citations.quote:
This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the manifold-product and tangent-bundle suppliers cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with its
induced smooth structure ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]), and let
$M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$, equivalently the tuple $(M,g,N)$ with $N$ as in
clause (d). That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.
The Euclidean inclusion of $S^n$ induces its round metric. In spherical coordinates on $S^2$, $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.

Let $(M,\mathcal S)$ and $(N,\mathcal T)$ be smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$
and $n$. Then $M\times N$ with the product topology is a topological
$(m+n)$-manifold. If $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are smooth atlases with
$[\mathcal A]=\mathcal S$ and $[\mathcal B]=\mathcal T$, then the set of product
charts

$$\mathcal A\times\mathcal B:=\bigl\{\,\bigl(V\times W,\ \varphi\times\psi\bigr):(V,\varphi)\in\mathcal A,\ (W,\psi)\in\mathcal B\,\bigr\}$$

is a smooth atlas on $M\times N$, and the maximal atlas it generates is
independent of the presenting atlases: it depends only on $\mathcal S$ and
$\mathcal T$. This maximal atlas is the **product smooth structure** of
$M\times N$.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and let $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$ be a family
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor at $p$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Suppose that the component
functions of $A$ are $C^\infty$ in the charts of one smooth atlas of $M$. Let
$(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be overlapping smooth charts of the maximal smooth atlas and
let $A_{cd}$ and $A'_{ab}$ denote their coordinate representatives in the
charts $x$ and $y$ as specified in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]].
For $q\in U\cap V$ put $u=y(q)$ and write $x(u):=(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$. Then

$$A'_{ab}(u) = \sum_{c,d\in I_n}\frac{\partial x^c}{\partial y^a}(u)\,\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial y^b}(u)\,A_{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),$$

where $\partial x^c/\partial y^a$ are the entries of the total derivative
$D(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$; $I_n$ is the label set of the supplier,
so in dimension four the sum runs from $0$ through $3$. In particular $A$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
on $M$: its components are $C^\infty$ in every chart of the maximal smooth
atlas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and let $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$ be a family
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor at $p$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Suppose that the component
functions of $A$ are $C^\infty$ in the charts of one smooth atlas of $M$. Let
$(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be overlapping smooth charts of the maximal smooth atlas and
let $A_{cd}$ and $A'_{ab}$ denote their coordinate representatives in the
charts $x$ and $y$ as specified in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]].
For $q\in U\cap V$ put $u=y(q)$ and write $x(u):=(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$. Then

$$A'_{ab}(u) = \sum_{c,d\in I_n}\frac{\partial x^c}{\partial y^a}(u)\,\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial y^b}(u)\,A_{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),$$

where $\partial x^c/\partial y^a$ are the entries of the total derivative
$D(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$; $I_n$ is the label set of the supplier,
so in dimension four the sum runs from $0$ through $3$. In particular $A$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
on $M$: its components are $C^\infty$ in every chart of the maximal smooth
atlas.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: (Global smooth tensor.) The product manifold atlas covers $M$, including charts about both sphere poles, by [L2]. The projections $x^0,r,\iota$ are smooth, $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and $\gamma_{S^2}$ is a smooth covariant tensor on all of $S^2$ by [L1]-[L3]. Therefore each term of the coordinate-free expression in [L1] is a smooth tensor field on $M$, their sum is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field, and on the regular angular locus its polar components are the display of clause (a). By [L5], smooth changes of angular coordinates re-express this same tensor by the covariant component transformation law in the corresponding coordinate bases, including pole charts. This proves the global assertion and the chart-local statement.

(Nondegeneracy and inertia, including the poles.) At $p=(x^0,r,\omega)$ the product tangent space splits as $T_pM\cong\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R\oplus T_\omega S^2$. For $v=(a,b,w)$ in this splitting,
$g_p(v,v)=-f(r)a^2+f(r)^{-1}b^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2,\omega}(w,w)$.
Here $f(r)>0$, and $\gamma_{S^2,\omega}$ is positive definite at every sphere point, including the poles. The first two summands thus have one negative and one positive direction, and the sphere summand has two positive directions; $g_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$ at every $p$. This proves (b).

(Time orientation.) The product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth and nowhere zero. By [L1] and the global metric formula, $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ everywhere, so $N$ is a time orientation. The base-vector signs and the polar angular signs in (c) follow from that formula and the positive-definite round metric.

(Conclusion.) Step 1.1 proves (a), step 1.2 proves (b) at all sphere points, and step 2.1 proves (c). Clauses (d)-(e) record the polar-chart domain of the component display and the global scope of the tensor formula. No property outside $r>s$ is asserted.

boundaries.reason: The proof handles the points of one product chart and an arbitrary pair of overlapping charts on the nonempty manifold M; no union, sum or family indexed by an unbounded set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 exhibits the frame matrix diag(-f, 1/f, r^2, r^2 sin^2(theta)) and computes det g = -r^4 sin^2(theta): since f>0 for r>s and sin(theta) is nonzero on 0<theta<pi, no diagonal entry vanishes, so the zero-eigenvalue case is decided by the domain.

boundaries.reason: The claim is four-dimensional and treats a general product chart; no one-dimensional or single-patch specialization is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 computes the determinant and reads off the inertia from the diagonal signs, so nondegeneracy of g_p at every chart point is established and not assumed.

boundaries.reason: Product charts are open subsets of M with 0<theta<pi; the horizon value r=s and the poles theta=0,pi are outside every chart domain and are never evaluated in this proof.
No element is selected from a nonempty family: the chart pair whose overlap is checked is arbitrary, and each chart is part of the given datum.
Clauses (b) and (c) are asserted outright for the given metric; the lemma does not derive them from a hypothesis about an abstract manifold.
No converse is claimed: the lemma never asserts that every smooth time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with such components must be this datum.

citations.quote:
This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the manifold-product and tangent-bundle suppliers cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with its
induced smooth structure ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]), and let
$M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$, equivalently the tuple $(M,g,N)$ with $N$ as in
clause (d). That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $r,s\ge0$ be integers.

**(a) Tensors at a point.** For $p\in M$, the tangent space $T_pM$ is the real
vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]) and the cotangent space is
its algebraic dual, $T_p^*M=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]). A **type
$(r,s)$ tensor at $p$** is a multilinear map

$$T_p:(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

in the sense of [[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]:
the first $r$ arguments are covectors and the last $s$ are vectors. In
particular a type $(1,0)$ tensor is a vector, a type $(0,1)$ tensor is a
covector and a type $(0,2)$ tensor is a bilinear form, so the covariant
$2$-tensors of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] are exactly the
type $(0,2)$ tensors of this definition.

**(b) The tensor bundle and smooth fields.** The **type $(r,s)$ tensor bundle**
$T^r_sM$ is the disjoint union of the fibres $T^r_sM|_p=\operatorname{Mult}((T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s,\mathbb R)$
over $p\in M$ ([[def-type-r-s-tensor-bundle]]); it carries the smooth
vector-bundle structure defined by the tensor-coordinate change rules
([[thm-tensor-transition-laws-define-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]). A **smooth
tensor field of type $(r,s)$** on $M$ is a family $T=(T_p)_{p\in M}$ assigning
to each $p$ a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$, such that for every smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas the **component functions**

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}(q):=T_q\bigl(dx^{a_1}|_q,\dots,dx^{a_r}|_q,\ \partial_{b_1}|_q,\dots,\partial_{b_s}|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$; here the coordinate derivations
$\partial_b|_q=\partial/\partial x^b|_q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]) and the
coordinate differentials $dx^a|_q$ form the dual basis of $T_q^*M$
([[thm-coordinate-differentials-form-the-dual-cotangent-basis]]). This is
equivalent to $T$ being a smooth section of $T^r_sM$ in the sense of
[[def-smooth-tensor-field]]: the component functions are the frame
coefficients of the section in the local frame induced by the chart. The
smoothness condition is independent of the chosen smooth atlas and the
components in two overlapping charts are related by the transformation law
proved in the lemma on this page; the definition is therefore chart
independent rather than merely chart-wise.

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices are written $a,b,c,\dots$ for components in
a chart, with the Einstein summation convention: a repeated index, once upper
and once lower, is summed over $0,1,2,3$. An upper index is a contravariant
slot in which a covector is evaluated, a lower index a covariant slot in which
a vector is evaluated. Slots are moved between these positions with the
musical isomorphisms $\flat_p,\sharp_p$ of
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]; for example, lowering the
first slot of a type $(1,1)$ field uses $(g^\flat T)^a{}_b=g_{ac}T^c{}_b$ and
raising uses $g^{ac}$. This is an identification of slots, not a change of the
field into a field of another kind, and it uses the metric nondegeneracy.

**(d) Scope.** The definition is purely local and chart-based; no global
triviality of $T^r_sM$, no global frame and no choice of metric-compatible
fields is assumed or implied. All fields are smooth ($C^\infty$); no
lower-regularity or distributional tensor field is defined here. The smooth
structure of the tangent bundle, and hence of $T^r_sM$
([[thm-tensor-transition-laws-define-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]), inherits the
axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] recorded with
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the component formulation of smoothness
itself makes no choice.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on
$M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) and let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, with Christoffel symbols $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a
\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]])
and metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$. Then:

1. $\nabla$ is torsion-free ([[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]])
   if and only if $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ for all $a,b,c$ in every
   smooth chart.
2. $\nabla$ is $g$-compatible ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) if and
   only if, in every smooth chart,

$$\partial_ag_{bc}=\sum_{d=0}^{3}\bigl(\Gamma^d{}_{ab}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{bd}\bigr) \qquad(a,b,c=0,1,2,3).$$

Thus $\nabla$ is metric-selected for $(M,g)$ if and only if both displayed
conditions hold in every smooth chart.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

derivations.claim: (Metric derivatives and inverse components.) The only nonconstant components of [L1] are $g_{00}=-f(r)$, $g_{11}=f(r)^{-1}$, $g_{22}=r^2$, $g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$, and their nonzero coordinate derivatives are $\partial_1g_{00}=-f'$, $\partial_1g_{11}=-f'/f^2$, $\partial_1g_{22}=2r$, $\partial_1g_{33}=2r\sin^2\vartheta$, $\partial_2g_{33}=2r^2\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$; by [L4] every $\partial_0$ or $\partial_3$ derivative vanishes. The inverse components are $g^{00}=-1/f$, $g^{11}=f$, $g^{22}=1/r^2$, $g^{33}=1/(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)$, as the diagonal matrix inverse of [L2].

(The family $\Gamma^0{}_{\cdot\cdot}$.) By [L3], $\Gamma^0{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{00}(\partial_bg_{0c}+\partial_cg_{0b}-\partial_0g_{bc})$. If $\{b,c\}$ contains an index in $\{2,3\}$ then $g_{0c}$ or $g_{0b}$ vanishes identically and $\partial_0g_{bc}=0$; the cases $(b,c)=(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ give $\partial_0g_{00}=0$ and $\partial_0g_{11}=0$; hence only $(b,c)\in\{(0,1),(1,0)\}$ can contribute, with value $\tfrac12g^{00}\partial_1g_{00}=\tfrac12(-1/f)(-f')=f'/(2f)$. This is claim (a).

(The family $\Gamma^1{}_{\cdot\cdot}$.) By [L3], $\Gamma^1{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{11}(\partial_bg_{1c}+\partial_cg_{1b}-\partial_1g_{bc})$. If $g_{1c}$ or $g_{1b}$ is nonzero the corresponding term contributes; since $g_{1d}=0$ unless $d=1$, only $b=c=1$ retains a contribution and $\Gamma^1{}_{11}=\tfrac12g^{11}\partial_1g_{11}=\tfrac12f(-f'/f^2)=-f'/(2f)$. The cases $(b,c)=(0,0)$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$ have $\Gamma^1{}_{bc}=-\tfrac12g^{11}\partial_1g_{bc}$, giving $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\tfrac12f f'=ff'/2$, $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-\tfrac12f(2r)=-rf$ and $\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta$. Every mixed case $(b\ne c)$ has $\partial_bg_{1c}+\partial_cg_{1b}=0$ and $\partial_1g_{bc}=0$ for the off-diagonal components, hence vanishes. This is claim (b).

(The families $\Gamma^2{}_{\cdot\cdot}$ and $\Gamma^3{}_{\cdot\cdot}$.) For the upper index $2$, [L3] gives $\Gamma^2{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{22}(\partial_bg_{2c}+\partial_cg_{2b}-\partial_2g_{bc})$ with $g^{22}=1/r^2$. The only nonzero $g_{2c}$ is $c=2$, so only $b=c=2$ and the pairs with $g_{bc}$ depending on $\vartheta$ contribute: $\Gamma^2{}_{22}=\tfrac12r^{-2}\partial_2g_{22}=0$ and $\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\tfrac12r^{-2}\partial_2g_{33}=-\tfrac12r^{-2}(2r^2\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta)=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$, while $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\tfrac12r^{-2}\partial_1g_{22}=r^{-2}\cdot r=1/r$ and the $(0,0)$ case vanishes. For the upper index $3$, $g^{33}=1/(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)$ and only $g_{33}$ is nonzero among the $g_{3c}$: $\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\tfrac12(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_1g_{33}=\tfrac12(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)^{-1}(2r\sin^2\vartheta)=1/r$, $\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\tfrac12(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_2g_{33}=\tfrac12(r^2\sin^2\vartheta)^{-1}(2r^2\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta)=\cot\vartheta$, and $\Gamma^3{}_{33}=\tfrac12g^{33}\partial_3g_{33}=0$ by [L4]; all cases with an index $0$ or $1$ in $b,c$ other than the displayed ones vanish because the corresponding $g_{3c}$ or $g_{bc}$ is constant. Together with the lower-pair symmetry of [L3], these are claims (c) and (d).

(Exhaustiveness and the model values.) The index triples $(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ split into the families treated in step 1.1 and steps 2.1-2.3; each family was computed from the same unique connection $\nabla$ of [L1], so the displays (a)-(d) list exactly the nonzero symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart. Substituting $f=1-s/r$ and $f'=s/r^2$ of [L4] into the general expressions (a)-(d) gives the second display of the Statement. All symbols are smooth on the chart domain by [L5], and the expressions are those of the metric-selected connection, not of an arbitrary connection.

boundaries.reason: The computation is an exhaustive case check over the finitely many index triples in one chart; no indexed family, sum or union over an unbounded set is formed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 supplies the inverse components g^{00}=-1/f, g^{11}=f, g^{22}=1/r^2, g^{33}=1/(r^2 sin^2(theta)) and the nonzero derivatives, and step 3.1 verifies that precisely the listed triples are nonzero and all others vanish; the denominators f, r, sin(theta) are nonzero on the chart domain.

boundaries.reason: The symbols are listed for all index triples; no one-component or one-dimensional reduction is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 uses the inverse metric entries, whose existence requires f>0 and sin(theta) != 0 on the chart domain, so degenerate metrics cannot occur in the stated domain.

boundaries.reason: No endpoint of the domain r>s or of the angular interval (0,pi) is evaluated; the symbols are computed on open chart domains only.
The index bookkeeping is finite and explicit; nothing is chosen from a nonempty family of sets.
The item computes the symbols of the given metric-selected connection; it asserts no implication from some equivalence.
The list does not characterize which four-dimensional metrics have these Christoffel symbols; no converse is stated.

citations.quote:
Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let $\nabla$ be
the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). In every
spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ with
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$, the
Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) are:

**(a)** $\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, and
$\Gamma^0{}_{00}=\Gamma^0{}_{11}=\Gamma^0{}_{ij}=0$ for all remaining index
pairs;

**(b)** $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\dfrac{ff'}{2}$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta$, and
$\Gamma^1{}_{01}=\Gamma^1{}_{02}=\Gamma^1{}_{03}=\Gamma^1{}_{12}=\Gamma^1{}_{13}=\Gamma^1{}_{23}=0$;

**(c)** $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $2$ vanishes;

**(d)** $\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $3$ vanishes.

All components not listed vanish; equivalently, the only nonzero symbols are
those displayed. For the model value $f(r)=1-s/r$, so that $f'=s/r^2$, the
listed symbols read

$$\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\frac{s}{2r^2 f},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{00}=\frac{s f}{2r^2},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\frac{s}{2r^2f},$$

$$\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf,\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\frac{1}{r},\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^3{}_{23}=\cot\vartheta .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.
