**(d) Scope.** The acceleration and the expansion are geometric data of the
congruence $n$ alone, computed with the connection $\nabla$. This item asserts
neither $a=0$ (a geodesic congruence) nor $\theta=0$, and it defines no shear,
vorticity, measurement, clock reading or physical interpretation; the reading
of observer curves as ideal-clock worldlines belongs to the framework's
postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$, let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open
subset and let $n$ be a smooth observer congruence on $U$, with acceleration
$a=\nabla_nn$, expansion $\theta=\nabla_an^a$ and along-congruence derivative
$D$ as in [[def-gr-congruence-acceleration-and-expansion]]. Then:

**(a) The acceleration is spatial.** $a$ is smooth and

$$g_p(a_p,n_p)=0\qquad\text{for every }p\in U,$$

that is, $a_p\in n_p^{\perp}$; equivalently $h(a)=a$ for the projection field
$h$ of [[def-gr-observer-energy-momentum-current]].

**(b) Acceleration of the observer curves.** Let $\gamma:I\to U$ be an
observer curve of the congruence, that is, an integral curve of $n$
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]] clause (b)), and let
$D_s$ denote the covariant derivative along $\gamma$
([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]). Then

$$D_s\gamma'(s)=a_{\gamma(s)}\qquad\text{for every }s\in I .$$

Consequently every observer curve is a geodesic in its flow parameter if and
only if $a=0$ on $U$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(c) Divergence form of the expansion.** In every smooth chart of $U$, with
$g_{ab}$ the metric components and $w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0$,

$$\theta=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,n^a\bigr),$$

and $\theta=g^{ab}\nabla_an_b=h^{ab}\nabla_an_b$ with
$h^{ab}=g^{ab}+n^an^b$. In particular $\theta$ is smooth.

**(d) Derivation property.** For smooth functions $f,h:U\to\mathbb R$,
$D(fh)=f\,Dh+h\,Df$, and $D$ annihilates constants.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For $a<c<b$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(c)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(c)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty
open subset, carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field
$n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that
$n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly,

$$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$

Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing. A single observer
at a point is therefore not a congruence, and a congruence is not an ordered
basis or frame of $T_qM$.

**(b) Observer curves.** Because $n$ is a smooth vector field on $U$, the
theorem on maximal integral curves
([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]) assigns to every $q\in U$ a unique
maximal integral curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$,
defined on an open interval $I_q\subseteq\mathbb R$. We call these curves the
**observers** (or **observer curves**) of the congruence. Each observer is
regular: $\gamma_q'(s)=n_{\gamma_q(s)}$ and $\lVert n\rVert_g=1$ at every
parameter value, so the tangent vector is unit timelike and future-directed at
every parameter value. Completeness of the maximal intervals $I_q$, and global
product or foliation structure of $U$, are not asserted. The parameter $s$ is
the flow parameter of $n$; it is not identified with any clock reading here.

**(c) Adapted charts.** An **$n$-adapted chart** is a smooth chart
$(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U'\to\mathbb R^4$ of $M$ whose domain $U'$ is a nonempty
open subset of $U$ and whose **spatial coordinates** $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant
along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U'$; equivalently, for every
$q\in U'$ the observer curve $\gamma_q$ satisfies
$u^i(\gamma_q(s))=u^i(q)$ for all $s$ with $\gamma_q(s)\in U'$ and
$i=1,2,3$. No global adapted chart, and no adapted chart on all of $U$, is
asserted by this definition; one exists near every point of $U$ by the
existence corollary proved on this page.

**(d) Scope.** A congruence is a field of observer directions on an open set; it
is not a chart, not a tetrad field, and not a family of parametrized
worldlines with specified domains. The physical reading of its observer curves
as ideal-clock worldlines, and the identification of the flow parameter with a
measurable time, belong to the physical postulates of the framework and are not
asserted here.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: (Unit timelike and future-directed.) By [L1] and [L4], $g(n,n)=f^{-1}g_{00}=f^{-1}(-f)=-1$, and $g(n,N)=f^{-1/2}g(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-f^{1/2}<0$; hence $n$ is a unit timelike future-directed smooth field, i.e. an observer congruence, and $f^{1/2}$ is smooth and positive. This proves (a).

(Integral curves.) Because $n=f(r)^{-1/2}\partial_0$ and $f$ depends only on $r$, in any angular chart at the fixed sphere point, the components of $n$ are $n^0=f(r_0)^{-1/2}$, $n^1=n^2=n^3=0$ along the curve at constant $(r_0,\omega_0)$; the curve of clause (b) has tangent $n$ at every value of the parameter $\lambda$ and satisfies the initial condition at $\lambda=0$, so by uniqueness of maximal integral curves [L5] it is the maximal integral curve, defined for all $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ because the explicit formula is defined there. This proves (b).

(Proper time.) The tangent $\gamma'(\lambda)=n_{\gamma(\lambda)}$ has $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1$ by step 1.1, so by [L3] the proper-time density is $c^{-1}\sqrt{1}=1/c$, constant; integrating over a parameter interval of length $\Delta\lambda$ gives $\Delta\tau=\Delta\lambda/c$. Since $x^0$ increases by $\Delta x^0=f(r_0)^{-1/2}\Delta\lambda$ over that interval by step 1.2, we obtain $\Delta\lambda=f(r_0)^{1/2}\Delta x^0$ and hence $\Delta\tau=f(r_0)^{1/2}\Delta x^0/c=f(r_0)^{1/2}\Delta t$; the increment is positive for $\Delta x^0>0$, and $0<f<1$ on $r>s$. This proves (c).

(Clock-rate ratio and acceleration.) Dividing the identity of step 2.1 for $r_1$ by the same identity for $r_2$ over a common coordinate interval gives $\Delta	au_1/\Delta	au_2=\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$, which is (d). For the acceleration, by [L2] and [L1], $
abla_nn=f^{-1/2}
abla_{\partial_0}(f^{-1/2}\partial_0)=f^{-1/2} igl(\partial_0(f^{-1/2})\partial_0+f^{-1/2}\Gamma^a{}_{00}\partial_a igr)=f^{-1}\Gamma^1{}_{00}\partial_1=	frac12f'\partial_1$, where the first term vanishes because $f$ is independent of $x^0$; substituting $f'=s/r^2$ gives $a= rac{s}{2r^2}\partial_1$, which is spatial, nonzero and along $\partial_1$. This computation holds on the dense polar-chart locus. Both $
abla_nn$ and $s(2r^2)^{-1}\partial_r$ are smooth global vector fields, so their equality extends to the poles by continuity. This proves (e) globally.

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 prove clauses (a)-(e) as identities of the datum, using only its geometric data and the cited definitions; clause (f) records that the clock reading and the observer interpretation belong to the framework's postulates and that no measurement or empirical comparison is made.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 verifies g(n,n)=-1 at every point of the nonempty manifold M, whose points index the family of static worldlines of clause (b); the family case is realized and its properties are checked, not vacuous.
step 3.1 divides by f(r_0)>0 and by the flow-parameter increment, and computes the acceleration coefficient s/(2r^2) with r>s>0; no denominator vanishes on the stated domain.

boundaries.reason: The item concerns a one-parameter family of worldlines and a pair of radii r_1<r_2; no isolated single-curve specialization beyond that pair is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 proves the congruence is unit timelike everywhere, so no tangent of an integral curve is null or zero; the degenerate case is excluded on M.

boundaries.reason: The integral curves are defined for all real flow parameters by step 1.2 and the coordinate increments of clause (c) are arbitrary finite differences, so no endpoint of the parametrization is excluded or evaluated.
The congruence, its integral curves and the two radii are given data; no selection from a family of nonempty sets is made.
The clauses are equalities along the curves, not one direction of an equivalence.
No converse classifies all time-independent unit timelike fields on the datum.

citations.quote:
Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let $\nabla$ be
the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). In every
spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ with
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$, the
Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) are:

**(a)** $\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, and
$\Gamma^0{}_{00}=\Gamma^0{}_{11}=\Gamma^0{}_{ij}=0$ for all remaining index
pairs;

**(b)** $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\dfrac{ff'}{2}$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta$, and
$\Gamma^1{}_{01}=\Gamma^1{}_{02}=\Gamma^1{}_{03}=\Gamma^1{}_{12}=\Gamma^1{}_{13}=\Gamma^1{}_{23}=0$;

**(c)** $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $2$ vanishes;

**(d)** $\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $3$ vanishes.

All components not listed vanish; equivalently, the only nonzero symbols are
those displayed. For the model value $f(r)=1-s/r$, so that $f'=s/r^2$, the
listed symbols read

$$\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\frac{s}{2r^2 f},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{00}=\frac{s f}{2r^2},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\frac{s}{2r^2f},$$

$$\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf,\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\frac{1}{r},\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^3{}_{23}=\cot\vartheta .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]), and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector
field with compact support whose flow $\Phi_v$ is a global flow
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose:

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(u,v)=S(g,\varphi)$ for all $(u,v)$ in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection; its existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. For a
smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ write $D_t$ for the covariant derivative along
$\gamma$ of [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]] with respect to
$\nabla$ (equivalently, the pullback of the Levi–Civita connection).

1. **Metric pairing.** For smooth sections $V,W$ of the pullback bundle
   $\gamma^*TM$,
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\,g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),W(t)\bigr)=g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_tV(t),W(t)\bigr)+g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),D_tW(t)\bigr).$$
   In particular, if $D_tV=D_tW=0$ on $I$, then $g(V,W)$ is constant on $I$.

2. **Parallel transport.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise smooth curve.
   For every $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$ there is exactly one continuous piecewise
   smooth section $V$ of $\gamma^*TM$ with $D_tV=0$ on each smooth piece and
   $V(a)=v$; the parallel-transport map
   $P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(a)}M\to T_{\gamma(b)}M$, $v\mapsto V(b)$, is linear,
   bijective, and satisfies
   $g_{\gamma(b)}(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g_{\gamma(a)}(v,w)$ for all $v,w$.

3. **Geodesic speed and proper time.** Along a geodesic
   $\gamma:I\to M$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) the function
   $t\mapsto g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))$ is constant. If $\gamma$
   is nonconstant, its tangent is nowhere zero and its causal character
   (timelike, null or spacelike) is constant; a constant geodesic has zero
   tangent and is assigned none of those causal characters. If $\gamma$ is a
   **future-directed timelike geodesic** and
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$ with $\lambda>0$, then for
   $t_0<t_1$ its proper-time increment over $[t_0,t_1]$ is
   $\lambda(t_1-t_0)/c$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]), so proper time is an
   affine parameter. In this parameter its four-velocity is
   $U=(c/\lambda)\gamma'$ and is parallel: $D_\tau U=0$. Proper time is not
   assigned to a past-directed curve by that definition; reversing the
   parameter gives a future-directed timelike geodesic with the same
   (positive) proper-time magnitude. A nonconstant null geodesic has null
   tangent and admits no proper-time parametrization.

4. **Affine reparametrizations.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a geodesic whose
   tangent is nowhere zero, and let $h:J\to I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto
   its open image with $h'\neq0$. Then $\gamma\circ h$ is a geodesic if and
   only if $h(s)=as+b$ with constants $a\neq0$, $b$; in that case $a$ is the
   constant $h'$, and every affine parameter of this nonconstant geodesic
   arises in this way from a fixed one. If $\gamma$ is constant, then
   $\gamma\circ h$ is constant and hence geodesic for every such $h$; no
   affine restriction on $h$ follows.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For $a<c<b$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(c)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(c)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Define the
smooth vector field

$$n:=f^{-1/2}\,\partial_0=\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1/2}\partial_0$$

on $M$. Then:

**(a) Observer congruence.** $n$ is a smooth observer congruence on $M$ in the
sense of [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]: $g(n,n)=-1$ and
$g(n,N)<0$ at every point, so $n$ is a future-directed unit timelike field.

**(b) Integral curves.** For any $p=(c_0,r_0,\omega_0)\in M$, including sphere poles, the maximal integral curve of $n$ through $p$, with length-valued flow parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, is
$$\lambda\mapsto\bigl(c_0+f(r_0)^{-1/2}\lambda,\ r_0,\ \omega_0\bigr).$$
It is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and is the **static observer worldline** at radius $r_0$. In a spherical-polar chart it has constant angular coordinates $(\vartheta_0,\varphi_0)$; in any angular chart the sphere point is constant, and the global coordinate $x^0$ increases monotonically.

**(c) Proper time and clock rate.** Along each static observer worldline the
proper time $\tau$ is an affine function of the flow parameter $\lambda$, with
$\frac{d\tau}{d\lambda}=\frac1c$, and

$$\Delta\tau=\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{c}\,\Delta x^0=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t,$$

where $\Delta x^0$ is the coordinate difference in metres between two events
of the worldline and $\Delta t=\Delta x^0/c$ is the same difference in
seconds. In particular the proper-time increment is strictly positive for
$\Delta x^0>0$, and it is smaller than $\Delta t$ at every finite radius
because $0<f(r_0)<1$.

**(d) Clock-rate ratio.** For two static observers at radii
$r_1,r_2\in(s,\infty)$ compared over the same coordinate interval
$\Delta x^0$, the proper-time increments satisfy

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_1}{\Delta\tau_2}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_1)}{f(r_2)}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-s/r_1}{1-s/r_2}} .$$

**(e) Acceleration.** The acceleration field of the congruence is
$a:=\nabla_nn=\frac{f'(r)}{2}\,\partial_1=\frac{s}{2r^2}\,\partial_r$; it is
spatial, nowhere zero, and points in the direction of increasing $r$, so the
static observers are not geodesics.

**(f) Scope.** These are identities of the geometric datum. The reading of
$\tau$ as the time measured by an ideal clock and of the congruence as a
family of static observers belongs to the framework's postulates and is not
asserted here; no measurement and no comparison with any observed rate is
made.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

derivations.claim: (The fields $\partial_0$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are Killing.)
