For $\xi=\partial_0$ the lowered field is $\xi_b=g_{0b}=-f\delta^0_b$, and the Killing equation reads $\partial_ag_{0b}+\partial_bg_{0a}-2\Gamma^c{}_{ab}g_{0c}=0$; substituting [L1], the only potentially nonzero components are $(a,b)=(0,1)$: $\partial_1g_{00}+2f\Gamma^0{}_{01}=-f'+f'=0$, and $(a,b)=(0,0)$: $2\partial_0g_{00}=0$; all other components involve derivatives of vanishing components or vanishing symbols, so they vanish. For $\xi=\partial_\varphi$ the lowered field is $\xi_b=r^2\sin^2\vartheta\,\delta^3_b$, and the equation is $\partial_ag_{3b}+\partial_bg_{3a}-2r^2\sin^2\vartheta\,\Gamma^3{}_{ab}=0$; its potentially nonzero components are $(a,b)=(1,3)$: $2r\sin^2\vartheta-2r^2\sin^2\vartheta\cdot(1/r)=0$, $(a,b)=(2,3)$: $2r^2\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta-2r^2\sin^2\vartheta\cdot\cot\vartheta=0$, and $(a,b)=(3,3)$: $2\partial_3g_{33}=0$; all other components vanish. Hence both fields are Killing by [L2], and $e=-g(U,\partial_0)$ and $\ell=g(U,\partial_\varphi)$ are constant along $\gamma$. For positivity: $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$ is a future unit timelike field by [L5], and $-g(n,U)>0$; since $-g(n,U)=f^{-1/2}e$, we get $e>0$. This proves (a).

(Equatorial reduction.) The coordinate geodesic system [L3] and [L1] has the equations
$$\ddot x^0+\frac{f'}{f}\dot x^0\dot r=0,\quad \ddot r+\frac{ff'}2(\dot x^0)^2-\frac{f'}{2f}\dot r^2-rf\dot\vartheta^2-rf\sin^2\vartheta\dot\varphi^2=0,$$
$$\ddot\vartheta+\frac2r\dot r\dot\vartheta-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta\dot\varphi^2=0,\quad \ddot\varphi+\frac2r\dot r\dot\varphi+2\cot\vartheta\dot\vartheta\dot\varphi=0.$$
Set $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and $\dot\vartheta=0$ in the $x^0,r,\varphi$ equations.
The resulting smooth three-equation subsystem, written as a first-order
system for positions and velocities, has an open state domain containing the
initial data because $r(\tau_0)>s$ and the chosen product chart is open. Its
right-hand side is smooth and hence locally Lipschitz, so [L7] gives a local
solution with the same positions and velocities as $\gamma$ at $\tau_0$.
Adjoining the constant
coordinate $\vartheta=\pi/2$ gives a solution of the full four equations,
because the $\vartheta$ equation vanishes and the other equations reduce to
that subsystem. This constructed geodesic has the same event and tangent as
$\gamma$ at $\tau_0$, so uniqueness in [L3] makes them agree on a
neighborhood of $\tau_0$. Let
$$E:=\{\tau\in I:\vartheta(\tau)=\pi/2\text{ and }\dot\vartheta(\tau)=0\}.$$
It is nonempty, closed by continuity, and open by the same local construction
at each of its points. Since $I$ is an interval, $E=I$. Thus
$\vartheta\equiv\pi/2$ on $I$, proving (b); in particular
$\sin^2\vartheta=1$ there.

(Normalization identity.) By [L4], $-c^2=g(U,U)=-f(\dot x^0)^2+f^{-1}\dot r^2+r^2\dot\varphi^2$ on the equatorial geodesic. Substituting $\dot x^0=e/f$ and $\dot\varphi=\ell/r^2$ from the definitions of $e,\ell$ and multiplying by $f$ gives $-c^2f=-e^2+\dot r^2+f\ell^2/r^2$, that is, $\dot r^2=e^2-f(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)=e^2-W_\ell(r)$. This is the normalization identity of (c).

(Radial equation.) The $r$-component of the geodesic equation [L3] is, by [L1], $\ddot r+\tfrac{ff'}{2}(\dot x^0)^2-\tfrac{f'}{2f}\dot r^2-rf\dot\varphi^2=0$. Substituting $\dot x^0=e/f$ and $\dot\varphi=\ell/r^2$ turns this into $\ddot r+\tfrac{f'e^2}{2f}-\tfrac{f'}{2f}\dot r^2-\tfrac{f\ell^2}{r^3}=0$. The claimed equation reads, after substituting $W_\ell'$, $\ddot r+\tfrac{f'}{2}\bigl(c^2+\tfrac{\ell^2}{r^2}\bigr)-\tfrac{f\ell^2}{r^3}=0$. The difference between the two left-hand sides is $\tfrac{f'}{2f}\bigl(e^2-\dot r^2-f(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)\bigr)=\tfrac{f'}{2f}(e^2-\dot r^2-W_\ell(r))$, which vanishes precisely by the normalization identity of step 1.3; the substitution of $W_\ell'$ and the rearrangement use the derivative rules of [L6]. Hence, given that identity, the $r$-equation and $\ddot r=-\tfrac12W_\ell'$ are equivalent. This proves (c).

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 2.1 prove clauses (a)-(c) for the given geodesic on its chart interval; clause (d) records that the reduction is local and asserts nothing about completeness, extension or null geodesics.

boundaries.reason: The reduction is stated along one given geodesic on its chart interval; no indexed family or union over an unbounded set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.3 solves the normalization with f>0 and step 2.1 differentiates W_ell whose denominators r and r^3 are nonzero for r>s; the turning points where r-dot=0 are not divided by, and clause (c) asserts r-ddot=-W'/2 together with the normalization rather than by division by r-dot.

boundaries.reason: The geodesic is a curve in the four-manifold and no one-dimensional model is substituted for it.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.3 uses g(U,U)=-c^2 with c>0, so the tangent is nowhere null or zero; the degenerate (lightlike) case for this reduction is excluded by hypothesis and treated separately for null geodesics elsewhere.

clause (d) and step 3.1 restrict the statement to the interval on which the geodesic stays in one product chart with r>s and 0<theta<pi; endpoints of that interval and any extension beyond the chart are excluded explicitly.

boundaries.reason: A product chart containing the image of the geodesic is part of the hypotheses, and the constants e, ell are those of the given curve; no further selection is made.

boundaries.evidence: clause (c) states the equivalence, given the normalization identity, between the r-component of the geodesic equation and r-ddot=-W'/2; step 2.1 proves the forward direction by substituting the constants into the r-equation.

step 2.1 shows the difference of the two left-hand sides equals (f'/(2f))(e^2-r-dot^2-W_ell(r)), which vanishes by step 1.3, so the reduced equation conversely implies the r-component under the same identity.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let $\nabla$ be
the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). In every
spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ with
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$, the
Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) are:

**(a)** $\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, and
$\Gamma^0{}_{00}=\Gamma^0{}_{11}=\Gamma^0{}_{ij}=0$ for all remaining index
pairs;

**(b)** $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\dfrac{ff'}{2}$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta$, and
$\Gamma^1{}_{01}=\Gamma^1{}_{02}=\Gamma^1{}_{03}=\Gamma^1{}_{12}=\Gamma^1{}_{13}=\Gamma^1{}_{23}=0$;

**(c)** $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $2$ vanishes;

**(d)** $\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $3$ vanishes.

All components not listed vanish; equivalently, the only nonzero symbols are
those displayed. For the model value $f(r)=1-s/r$, so that $f'=s/r^2$, the
listed symbols read

$$\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\frac{s}{2r^2 f},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{00}=\frac{s f}{2r^2},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\frac{s}{2r^2f},$$

$$\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf,\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\frac{1}{r},\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^3{}_{23}=\cot\vartheta .$$

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a **future
timelike geodesic**, parametrized by proper time $\tau$, with tangent
$U=\gamma'$, so that $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future-directed
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] clause 3,
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Fix a spherical-polar product chart
$(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ containing the image of $\gamma$ and write a dot
for $\frac{d}{d\tau}$. Define

$$e:=-g(U,\partial_0)=f\dot x^0,\qquad \ell:=g(U,\partial_\varphi)=r^2\sin^2\vartheta\,\dot\varphi .$$

Then:

**(a) Conserved quantities.** $\partial_0$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are Killing
fields of $g$, and $e$ and $\ell$ are constant along $\gamma$; moreover
$e>0$.

**(b) Equatorial reduction.** Suppose $\vartheta(\tau_0)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and
$\dot\vartheta(\tau_0)=0$ at some $\tau_0\in I$. Then
$\vartheta(\tau)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ for all $\tau\in I$; the geodesic is
**equatorial**.

**(c) Radial reduction.** If $\gamma$ is equatorial, define the **effective
potential**

$$W_\ell(r):=f(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr).$$

Then the normalization identity

$$\dot r^2=e^2-W_\ell(r)$$

holds at every $\tau\in I$, and, given this identity, the $r$-component of the
geodesic equation is equivalent to the one-dimensional equation

$$\ddot r=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),\qquad W_\ell'(r)=f'(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr)-2f(r)\frac{\ell^2}{r^3}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The reduction is local: it is stated on the interval $I$ on
which the geodesic stays in one product chart with $r>s$ and
$0<\vartheta<\pi$; no completeness, no extension of $\gamma$ beyond $I$, and
no statement about null geodesics is made. The quantities $e$ and $\ell$ are
constants of the given geodesic, not functions of the model.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]), and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector
field with compact support whose flow $\Phi_v$ is a global flow
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose:

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(u,v)=S(g,\varphi)$ for all $(u,v)$ in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

derivations.claim: (The stationarity equation.) By [L2] and [L4], $W_\ell'(r)=f'(r)(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)-2f(r)\ell^2/r^3=\frac{s}{r^2}\bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\bigr)-2\bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\bigr)\frac{\ell^2}{r^3}$. Multiplying by $r^3/s$ gives $r c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r}-2\frac{\ell^2}{s}\bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\bigr)=rc^2+\frac{3\ell^2}{r}-\frac{2\ell^2}{s}$, so $W_\ell'(r)=0$ if and only if $\ell^2\bigl(\frac{2}{s}-\frac{3}{r}\bigr)=rc^2$, that is, $\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr^2}{2r-3s}$; this has a positive solution for $\ell^2$ precisely when $r>3s/2$, and the value is unique. This is the condition displayed in clauses (a) and (b).

(The timelike circular geodesic.) Let $r_0>3s/2$, choose $\ell$ as in (a) and $e=\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)}>0$, and define the global curve $\gamma$ of clause (a). At any parameter value choose a spherical-polar chart near its angular point; the local tangent components are $U^a=(e/f(r_0),0,0,\ell/r_0^2)$. Then $g(U,U)=-f(r_0)\bigl(e/f(r_0)\bigr)^2+r_0^2\bigl(\ell/r_0^2\bigr)^2=-\frac{e^2}{f(r_0)}+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}=-\bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\bigr)+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}=-c^2$ by the choice of $e$, so $U$ is timelike; and $g(U,\partial_0)=-e<0$, so $U$ is future-directed. In that chart the $x^0$-equation reduces to $\ddot x^0=0$ because $\dot r=0$; the $\vartheta$-equation reads $0+0-\sin(\pi/2)\cos(\pi/2)(\ell/r_0^2)^2=0$; the $\varphi$-equation reduces to $\ddot\varphi=0$ because $\dot r=\dot\vartheta=0$; and the $r$-equation reads $\frac{ff'}{2}\bigl(\frac{e}{f}\bigr)^2-rf\bigl(\frac{\ell}{r_0^2}\bigr)^2=\frac{f'e^2}{2f}-\frac{f\ell^2}{r_0^3}=\frac{f'}{2}\bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\bigr)-\frac{f\ell^2}{r_0^3}=\frac12W_\ell'(r_0)=0$, using the choice of $e$ in the third equality and step 1.1 in the last. These equations hold in every local chart interval along the curve; longitude charts differ by constant shifts, so the global curve is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ by [L3]. By [L5] and [L6], the global time translations and rotations are isometries, so $\partial_0$ and $\Phi$ are Killing; their pairings with $U$ are $-e$ and $\ell$. The Killing-pairing identity in [L5] proves these quantities are constant on the connected parameter interval. The local angular velocity is $\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\dot\varphi}{\dot x^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}$; squaring and substituting $\ell^2$ and $e^2=f(r_0)(c^2+\ell^2/r_0^2)$ gives $\bigl(\frac{\ell f}{r_0^2e}\bigr)^2=\frac{\ell^2f^2}{r_0^4f(c^2+\ell^2/r_0^2)}=\frac{\ell^2 f}{r_0^4c^2+r_0^2\ell^2}=\frac{s}{2r_0^3}$, using $\ell^2=c^2sr_0^2/(2r_0-3s)$; with $t=x^0/c$ this is $\bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\bigr)^2=c^2\frac{s}{2r_0^3}=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3}$. This proves (a).

(Necessity.) If an equatorial future timelike geodesic has $r\equiv r_0$ on an interval of positive length, then $\dot r=\ddot r=0$ there, so by [L2] $0=\ddot r=-\tfrac12W_\ell'(r_0)$ and step 1.1 gives $\ell^2=c^2sr_0^2/(2r_0-3s)$ and $r_0>3s/2$; the same conclusion holds on the whole parameter interval by the conservation of $\ell$ and continuity. This proves (b).

(The second derivative at fixed angular momentum.) Differentiate $W_\ell(x)=f(x)(c^2+\ell^2/x^2)$ twice while holding $\ell$ constant. This gives $W_\ell''(x)=f''(x)(c^2+\ell^2/x^2)-4f'(x)\ell^2/x^3+6f(x)\ell^2/x^4$. Only after this differentiation set $x=r$ and $\ell^2=\ell_r^2=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$. Substituting $f'=s/r^2$, $f''=-2s/r^3$ and simplifying gives $W_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{2c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)}$, hence $V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)}$, whose sign is that of $r-3s$. This proves (c).

(The photon sphere.) Let $\ell\ne0$, $r_0=3s/2$ and $e_0=\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}/r_0>0$; define the global curve $\eta$ of clause (d), with local tangent components $U^a=(e_0/f(r_0),0,0,\ell/r_0^2)$. Then $g(U,U)=-\frac{e_0^2}{f(r_0)}+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}=-\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}=0$, so $U$ is null; and $g(U,\partial_0)=-e_0<0$, so $U$ is future-directed. The local $x^0$-, $\vartheta$- and $\varphi$-equations hold as in step 2.1; the $r$-equation reads $\frac{f'e_0^2}{2f}-r_0f\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^4}=\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\bigl(\frac{f'}{2}-\frac{f}{r_0}\bigr)=\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^4}\bigl(\frac{3s}{2}-r_0\bigr)=0$ at $r_0=3s/2$. These local equations establish a future null geodesic on the entire domain $\mathbb R$ by [L3]. By [L5] and [L6], the global Killing fields have pairings $-e_0$ and $\ell$, constant along $\eta$. Its angular velocity is $\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}$, equal to $+\frac{2}{3\sqrt3\,s}$ for $\ell>0$ and to its negative for $\ell<0$, with square $4/(27s^2)$. Finally $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r)=f\ell^2/r^2$ has $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(r)=\ell^2\frac{-2r+3s}{r^4}$ (that is, $\ell^2(3s-2r)/r^4$), which vanishes at $r=3s/2$, and $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(r)=\ell^2\frac{6(r-2s)}{r^5}$, which at $r=3s/2$ equals $-\frac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$. This proves (d).

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1-3.1 prove clauses (a)-(d) from the metric data and the geodesic equations; clause (e) records the exact scope: the statements are about ideal geodesics of the model on $r>s$, with stability understood as the sign of the potential's second derivative, and no empirical or nonlinear claim is made.

boundaries.reason: The computations are for explicit radii and explicit curves in the four-manifold; no family indexed by an unbounded set is formed.

boundaries.evidence: steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 divide by 2r_0-3s, r_0^2, r_0^3 and 2r_0-3s with r_0>3s/2, so r_0>0 and 2r_0-3s>0; the limit r_0 down to 3s/2 is treated as a limit and not as a value at which a division is performed.

boundaries.reason: No one-dimensional or unit-mass specialization is asserted; the orbital data are for the stated s>0.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 constructs the curve with g(gamma',gamma')=-c^2 and step 1.1 verifies the stationarity equation with l^2>0, so the circular geodesic is nowhere null; the degenerate null limit at the photon sphere is treated in clause (d) as a separate null orbit.

the threshold r_0=3s/2 is handled as a limit in clause (b) and the strictly larger domain r_0>3s/2 is used wherever l^2 is formed; the ISCO value r_0=3s is evaluated by step 2.3 without division by the vanishing second derivative, which is computed to be zero.

boundaries.reason: The radius r_0, the curve and the constants of clause (a) are explicitly given; no nonempty family is selected from.
Clauses (a) and (d) assert existence of the explicit curves; the existence-to-condition direction is clause (b), a one-way implication, and no biconditional is claimed as such.
The item does not claim that every circular orbit of every radius arises from the displayed one-parameter formula beyond the necessity computation of clause (b).

citations.quote:
This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the manifold-product and tangent-bundle suppliers cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters.** Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$ and $m_*>0$ be the constants and mass
parameter of the Schwarzschild exterior datum, and put
$s:=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)). The
**Kruskal model datum of mass parameter $m_*$** is constructed from these
data as follows.

**(b) Domain and smooth structure.** Let
$\Omega:=\{(U,V)\in\mathbb R^2:UV<1\}$ and let
$\mathcal K:=\Omega\times S^2$, where $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ is the unit
Euclidean sphere, with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]],
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). It is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary. Write $U,V:\mathcal K\to\mathbb R$ for the first two
projections and $\iota:\mathcal K\to S^2$ for the third. A **Kruskal product
chart** uses any smooth chart on $S^2$. In a spherical-polar Kruskal chart the
angular coordinates satisfy $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and
$\gamma_{S^2}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sin^2\vartheta)_{ij}$; these charts omit
the two poles, which are covered by ordinary sphere charts.

**(c) The radial function.** The datum carries a function
$r:\mathcal K\to(0,\infty)$, the **Kruskal radial function**, characterized by
the implicit relation

$$U\,V=-\Bigl(\frac{r}{s}-1\Bigr)e^{r/s}\qquad\text{at every point of }\mathcal K .$$

That for every $(U,V)\in\Omega$ there is exactly one $r(U,V)>0$ satisfying
this relation, and that $r$ is smooth, is not asserted here; it is proved in
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]] on this page, the justification record of
this definition. The value $r=0$ is not attained on $\mathcal K$, and
$r=s$ exactly on the axes $U=0$ or $V=0$.

**(d) The metric.** Define the metric globally by

$$g_{\mathcal K}=-\frac{2s^3}{r}e^{-r/s}(dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU)+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar Kruskal chart its component functions are

$$g_{UV}:=g_{VU}:=-\frac{2s^3}{r}e^{-r/s},\qquad g_{\vartheta\vartheta}:=r^2,\qquad g_{\varphi\varphi}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{UU}:=g_{VV}:=g_{U\vartheta}:=g_{U\varphi}:=g_{V\vartheta}:=g_{V\varphi}:=0,$$

where $r$ is the function of clause (c) evaluated at the point. This global
expression defines a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on
$\mathcal K$ once the smoothness of $r$ is established by
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]]. In another sphere chart the angular block
is $r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. That $g_{\mathcal K}$ is Lorentzian is proved, not
asserted, in the same lemma.

**(e) Time orientation.** Define the field
$N_{\mathcal K}:=\partial_U+\partial_V$ on $\mathcal K$. Its component
expression is the same in every Kruskal chart; that it is a smooth timelike
field and hence a time orientation of $g_{\mathcal K}$ is proved in
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]].

**(f) Scope.** The datum is a geometric object: the definition asserts
nothing about whether $g_{\mathcal K}$ satisfies any field equation, about
its causal structure, about the maximality of the extension it provides, or
about nature. The comparison with the exterior datum, the vacuum property and
the causal structure are the content of the two following items on this page.
The region $\{UV=1\}$, where the implicit relation of clause (c) has no
solution with $r>0$, is not part of $\mathcal K$ and is not appended to it by
this definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.
The Euclidean inclusion of $S^n$ induces its round metric. In spherical coordinates on $S^2$, $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the manifold-product and tangent-bundle suppliers cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with its
induced smooth structure ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]), and let
$M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$, equivalently the tuple $(M,g,N)$ with $N$ as in
clause (d). That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Let
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2$ carry the product
smooth structure and let $\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}:M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to S^2$ be the
third projection. Its product atlas includes ordinary sphere charts at the
poles ([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]).
Define the **tortoise function**

$$r_*(r):=r+s\log\left|\frac{r}{s}-1\right|,\qquad r>0,\ r\ne s,$$

on each of the two intervals $(0,s)$ and $(s,\infty)$, and define the
**advanced-chart metric** globally on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$ by

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^2\,\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In spherical-polar product charts its components are

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\,d\Omega^2,$$

namely $g_{vv}=-f$, $g_{vr}=g_{rv}=1$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all
other components zero. In another sphere chart the angular block is
$r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. Then:

**(a) Smooth Lorentzian metric.** $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and at every point it is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; hence $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$
is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on all of
$r>0$, including $r=s$.

**(b) Time orientation.** The smooth vector field

$$N_{\mathrm{ext}}:=A(r)\,\partial_v-\partial_r,\qquad A(r):=\frac{f(r)+\sqrt{f(r)^2+4}}{2}>0,$$

satisfies $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},N_{\mathrm{ext}})<0$ everywhere
and $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},\partial_v)<0$ everywhere; hence
$N_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a time orientation of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and on the
region $r>s$ it determines the same future cone as the datum's time
orientation $\partial_v=\partial_0$.

**(c) Isometric embedding of the exterior.** The map
$\Phi:M\to M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, $(x^0,r,\omega)\mapsto(x^0+r_*(r),r,\omega)$
restricts to a diffeomorphism of $M$ onto the open subset $\{r>s\}$ of
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and $\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{ext}}=g$; the exterior datum is
therefore isometric to the region $r>s$ of the extension.

**(d) Vacuum and Kretschmann scalar of the extension.** The
metric-selected connection of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ exists and is unique, its
Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor vanish identically on
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and its Kretschmann scalar equals

$$R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}$$

on all of $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$. In particular the scalar is smooth and finite on
the horizon $r=s$, where it takes the value $12/s^4$.

**(e) The horizon is a null hypersurface.** The level set $\{r=s\}$ is a
smooth null hypersurface of $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$ whose null
generator direction is $\partial_v$; every smooth product-chart frame remains
a basis across $r=s$. In spherical-polar charts
$\det(g_{\mathrm{ext}})=-r^4\sin^2\vartheta$; in an arbitrary sphere chart
the determinant is $-r^4\det(\gamma_{ij})$, which is nonzero.

**(f) Scope.** The extension constructed here is a smooth Lorentzian
manifold containing the exterior isometrically and regular across $r=s$; it
is not claimed to be maximal, and no uniqueness or global structure theorem
is asserted. The region $r\le0$ and the surfaces relevant to the Kruskal
model of this page are outside this statement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let $\nabla$ be
the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). In every
spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ with
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$, the
Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) are:

**(a)** $\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, and
$\Gamma^0{}_{00}=\Gamma^0{}_{11}=\Gamma^0{}_{ij}=0$ for all remaining index
pairs;

**(b)** $\Gamma^1{}_{00}=\dfrac{ff'}{2}$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\dfrac{f'}{2f}$, $\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf$,
$\Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta$, and
$\Gamma^1{}_{01}=\Gamma^1{}_{02}=\Gamma^1{}_{03}=\Gamma^1{}_{12}=\Gamma^1{}_{13}=\Gamma^1{}_{23}=0$;

**(c)** $\Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^2{}_{21}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $2$ vanishes;

**(d)** $\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\Gamma^3{}_{31}=\dfrac{1}{r}$,
$\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, and every other symbol with
upper index $3$ vanishes.

All components not listed vanish; equivalently, the only nonzero symbols are
those displayed. For the model value $f(r)=1-s/r$, so that $f'=s/r^2$, the
listed symbols read

$$\Gamma^0{}_{01}=\Gamma^0{}_{10}=\frac{s}{2r^2 f},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{00}=\frac{s f}{2r^2},\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{11}=-\frac{s}{2r^2f},$$

$$\Gamma^1{}_{22}=-rf,\qquad \Gamma^1{}_{33}=-rf\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{12}=\Gamma^3{}_{13}=\frac{1}{r},\qquad \Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta,\qquad \Gamma^3{}_{23}=\cot\vartheta .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and curvature data $R^a{}_{bcd}$, $R_{abcd}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$, $G_{ab}$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In every spherical-polar
product chart
$(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$, writing $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$ and
$f''=\frac{d^2f}{dr^2}=-2s/r^3$:

**(a) Curvature components.** All nonzero components of the lowered
curvature tensor, up to the symmetries of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$R_{0101}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad R_{0202}=\frac{rf f'}{2},\qquad R_{0303}=\frac{rf f'\sin^2\vartheta}{2},$$

$$R_{1212}=-\frac{rf'}{2f},\qquad R_{1313}=-\frac{rf'\sin^2\vartheta}{2f},\qquad R_{2323}=r^2\bigl(1-f\bigr)\sin^2\vartheta .$$

Every component whose index pairs do not coincide as unordered pairs, and
every component with an index repeated inside a pair, vanishes.

**(b) Ricci tensor.** The Ricci tensor has the diagonal components

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=f\Bigl(\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}\Bigr),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{11}=-\frac{1}{f}\Bigl(\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}\Bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{22}=1-f-rf',\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{33}=\bigl(1-f-rf'\bigr)\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and all mixed components $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ with $a\ne b$ vanish.

**(c) Vanishing for the model.** For $f(r)=1-s/r$ one has
$\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}=0$ and $1-f-rf'=0$; consequently

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=0,\qquad S=0,\qquad G_{ab}=0$$

on the regular angular locus and, as tensor identities, on all of $M$ by
smoothness and density. In particular the
Schwarzschild exterior metric is a Ricci-flat metric, and $G=0$ holds as an
identity of smooth tensor fields.

**(d) The curvature does not vanish.** The model is not locally flat. The
global base-field contraction $R_{0101}:=g(R(\partial_0,\partial_r)
\partial_r,\partial_0)$ equals $-s/r^3$ on the regular angular locus, hence
everywhere by smoothness and density. It is therefore nowhere zero even
though the Ricci and Einstein tensors vanish identically.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with curvature data as in
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]]. On each spherical-polar
product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ define the local frame field

$$e_{\hat0}:=f^{-1/2}\partial_0,\qquad e_{\hat1}:=f^{1/2}\partial_1,\qquad e_{\hat2}:=r^{-1}\partial_2,\qquad e_{\hat3}:=(r\sin\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_3,$$

and for the curvature tensor define the **frame components**

$$\hat R_{\hat a\hat b\hat c\hat d}:=g\bigl(R(e_{\hat c},e_{\hat d})e_{\hat b},e_{\hat a}\bigr).$$

Then:

**(a) The frame field.** $(e_{\hat0},e_{\hat1},e_{\hat2},e_{\hat3})$ is a
smooth $g$-orthonormal frame (tetrad field) on the chart domain, with
$g(e_{\hat a},e_{\hat b})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\hat a\hat b}$, and
$e_{\hat0}$ is future-directed timelike; it is a tetrad field in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. It is not a coordinate frame.

**(b) Frame components.** The nonzero frame components, up to the
symmetries $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}=-R_{abdc}=R_{cdab}$ of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$\hat R_{\hat0\hat1\hat0\hat1}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad \hat R_{\hat0\hat2\hat0\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat0\hat3\hat0\hat3}=\frac{f'}{2r},$$

$$\hat R_{\hat1\hat2\hat1\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat1\hat3\hat1\hat3}=-\frac{f'}{2r},\qquad \hat R_{\hat2\hat3\hat2\hat3}=\frac{1-f}{r^2},$$

with $f'=s/r^2$ and $f''=-2s/r^3$; all other frame components vanish.

**(c) Kretschmann scalar.** Define the global smooth scalar field
$K:=R_{abcd}R^{abcd}$, with indices raised by the inverse metric. On the
spherical-polar chart locus its component expression is

$$K=f''^2+\frac{4(f')^2}{r^2}+\frac{4(1-f)^2}{r^4},$$

and for the model function $f=1-s/r$ this is

$$K=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}=\frac{48\,G_N^2m_*^2}{c^4\,r^6}.$$

The scalar identity is first computed on the regular angular locus and holds
on all of $M$ by smoothness and density. Since $r>s$ on $M$, one has
$0<K=12s^2/r^6<12/s^4$ at every point; as $r\downarrow s$ the expression has
the finite boundary value $12/s^4$, and the expression $12s^2/r^6$, read as a
function of $r>0$, grows without bound as $r\downarrow0$.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma computes curvature data of the exterior datum on
$r>s$. The limit $r\downarrow s$ is the boundary value on $M$ of the smooth
expression $12s^2/r^6$; no value of the metric at $r=s$ or at $r=0$ is used
or asserted here, those regions being outside the datum (the regular
continuation across $r=s$ is the separate extension lemma of this page).

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $X$ be a connected topological space ([[def-connected-space]]) and let
$f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), $\mathbb{R}$
carrying its usual topology ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
[[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $f[X]$ is an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-interval]]).
2. **Intermediate values are attained.** If $p, q \in X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   satisfies $f(p) \le c \le f(q)$, then there is $x \in X$ with $f(x) = c$.

Claim 2 is the intermediate value theorem with no hypothesis on $X$ beyond
connectedness: no order, no metric, no interval. The classical statement for a
continuous $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is the special case $X = [a,b]$, that
subspace being connected by [[cor-connected-subsets-of-the-line]].

Let $Z$ be a topological space, let $D \subseteq Z$ be dense
([[def-dense-top]]), let $Y$ be Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let
$f, g : Z \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) with

$$f(d) = g(d) \qquad \text{for every } d \in D .$$

Then $f = g$.

So a continuous map into a Hausdorff space is determined by its restriction to
any dense subset of its domain. Nothing is asserted about *which* functions on
$D$ extend: the statement is about uniqueness of an extension, not existence.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

$$\exp:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$
is a bijection.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

derivations.claim: (The radial function.) By [L6], $\varphi(r)=(1-r/s)e^{r/s}$ is smooth with $\varphi'(r)=-\frac{r}{s^2}e^{r/s}<0$ for $r>0$, so $\varphi$ is strictly decreasing. Its limits are $1$ as $r\downarrow0$ and $-\infty$ as $r\to\infty$: for $x=r/s>1$, the defining exponential series gives $e^x\ge1+x$, so $(x-1)e^x\ge(x-1)(1+x)\to\infty$. By [L4] its image is exactly $(-\infty,1)$, hence it is a bijection. Its derivative never vanishes; the smooth inverse-function theorem gives a smooth local inverse at each point of the image, and bijectivity makes those local inverses agree with the global inverse. Thus $r=\varphi^{-1}\circ(UV)$ is defined and smooth on all of $\Omega$, justifying clause (c) of the datum. The level relation gives $r=s$ exactly when $UV=0$ and $r\downarrow0$ as $UV\uparrow1$. This proves (a).

(The metric and time orientation, including the poles.) The base block of the global tensor [L1] in $(U,V)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&b\\b&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $b=-2s^3e^{-r/s}/r<0$, so it is nondegenerate with one positive and one negative eigenvalue. The angular block $r^2\gamma_{S^2}$ is positive definite at every sphere point, including both poles. Thus the global metric has inertia $(3,1,0)$. For $N_{\mathcal K}=\partial_U+\partial_V$, $g_{\mathcal K}(N_{\mathcal K},N_{\mathcal K})=2b=-4s^3e^{-r/s}/r<0$ everywhere, so it is a time orientation. This proves (b).

(The isometry with the exterior.) On $\Omega_+=\{U<0,V>0\}$ define $U=-e^{-(x^0-r_*)/(2s)}$, $V=e^{(x^0+r_*)/(2s)}$ with the branch $r>s$ of $r_*$; then $UV=-e^{r_*/s}=-(r/s-1)e^{r/s}$ by [L2] (since $e^{r_*/s}=(r/s-1)e^{r/s}$ on $r>s$), so the function defined implicitly satisfies $r(U,V)=r$ and the map $\Psi_+$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\{U<0,V>0\}$ with inverse $(U,V,\omega)\mapsto(s\log(V/(-U)),\,r(U,V),\,\omega)$. Differentiating, $dU=-\frac{U}{2s}(dx^0-r_*'dr)$ and $dV=\frac{V}{2s}(dx^0+r_*'dr)$, hence $dU\,dV+dV\,dU=-\frac{UV}{2s^2}\bigl(dx^0\otimes dx^0-r_*'^2dr\otimes dr\bigr)$. Substituting into $g_{\mathcal K}$ and using $\frac{sUVe^{-r/s}}{r}=-f$ and $r_*'^2=f^{-2}$, the pulled-back metric is $-f\,d(x^0)^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2=g$; this is the computation of [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-extension-chart]] restricted to the exterior.
