The chart with global coordinates y on V is given and the sphere chart is fixed; no selection from a nonempty family is made.
Clauses (a)-(c) are computed identities, not one direction of an equivalence.
No converse classifies which four-dimensional metrics are warped products of this form.

citations.quote:
Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty open set with global coordinates
$y=(y^0,y^1)$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]),
let $(q_{AB})$ be a smooth symmetric $2\times2$ matrix of functions on $V$
with

$$\Delta_q(y):=\det\bigl(q_{AB}(y)\bigr)<0\qquad(y\in V),$$

so that $q$ is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $V$ whose value
at every point is nondegenerate with inertia $(1,1,0)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]
clause (a), [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ be
a smooth function. Indices $A,B,C,D$ run over $\{0,1\}$ and indices
$i,j,k,l$ over the sphere directions below. Define on $V$:

$$(q^{AB}):=(q_{AB})^{-1},\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\tfrac12\sum_Dq^{AD}\bigl(\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}\bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r:=\partial_A\partial_Br-\sum_C\Gamma^C{}_{AB}\,\partial_Cr, \qquad \Delta_qr:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad z:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\,\partial_Br .$$

Further define

$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\sum_E\bigl(\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}\bigr), \qquad R_{ABCD}:=\sum_Eq_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD},$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=\sum_{A,C}q^{AC}R_{ABCD},\qquad S_q:=\sum_{B,D}q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}.$$

Let $S^2:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean
sphere with its induced smooth structure and round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]],
[[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]), let
$M:=V\times S^2$ carry the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
and let $\pi:M\to V$ and $\iota:M\to S^2$ be the projections. Define the
global symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$g:=\pi^*q+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$$

on $M$, where $r$ in this formula is pulled back from $V$. In any product
chart $(y^0,y^1,\xi^2,\xi^3)$, let $\gamma_{ij}$ be the round-metric
components of the angular chart. The components of $g$ are

$$g_{AB}:=q_{AB},\qquad g_{Ai}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=r^2\,\gamma_{ij} \qquad(A,B\in\{0,1\},\ i,j\in\{2,3\}),$$

Then:

**(a) The metric.** The global pullback formula defines a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$; at every point it is nondegenerate
with inertia $(3,1,0)$, so
$(M,g)$ is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(b) Christoffel symbols.** Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection of
$g$, unique by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]
clause (b) ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), and let
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}$ be its Christoffel symbols in a product chart. Then
the only nonzero symbols, beyond the displayed lower-index symmetry
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}=\Gamma^\mu{}_{\rho\nu}$, are

$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}\ \text{of the first display},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{Aj}=\frac{\partial_Ar}{r}\,\delta^i{}_j,\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-r\,q^{AB}\partial_Br\,\gamma_{ij},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{jk}\ \text{the round-sphere symbols in the chosen chart},$$

In a spherical-polar chart these are $\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$
and $\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, with all other
$\Gamma^i{}_{jk}$ vanishing. Pole charts use their own round-metric symbols.

**(c) Ricci tensor.** With $\operatorname{Ric}$ the Ricci tensor of $\nabla$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (c)), in every product
chart

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}-\frac{2}{r}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{Ai}=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=\bigl(1-z-r\Delta_qr\bigr)\gamma_{ij}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The statements are identities of the displayed component
functions in product charts and use no field equation, no vacuum condition and
no sign or positivity assumption on $s$; nothing is asserted about
completeness, geodesics, extensions or the physical reading of the coordinates.
The hypothesis $\Delta_q<0$ is used for nondegeneracy and inertia of $g$; it is
the only signature input.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]), and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector
field with compact support whose flow $\Phi_v$ is a global flow
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose:

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(u,v)=S(g,\varphi)$ for all $(u,v)$ in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
(The two curvature antisymmetries.) Let $X,Y,Z,W$ be coordinate vector fields on $V$, so $[X,Y]=0$ by [[prop-coordinate-vector-fields-commute]]. The compatibility identity in [L1] says $Xq(Z,W)=q(\nabla_XZ,W)+q(Z,\nabla_XW)$ for the base connection defined by the displayed Christoffel symbols. Apply $X$ to the compatibility identity for $Yq(Z,W)$, apply $Y$ to the one for $Xq(Z,W)$, and subtract. The mixed terms cancel in pairs, and $XYq(Z,W)-YXq(Z,W)=0$; using the curvature definition in [L1] gives [L1, algebra]
$$q(R(X,Y)Z,W)+q(Z,R(X,Y)W)=0.$$
With $X=\partial_C$, $Y=\partial_D$, $Z=\partial_B$, $W=\partial_A$, this is $R_{ABCD}=-R_{BACD}$. The defining curvature formula also changes sign when $C,D$ are exchanged, so $R_{ABCD}=-R_{ABDC}$. In dimension two, a component can therefore be nonzero only if each of $(A,B)$ and $(C,D)$ is $(0,1)$ or $(1,0)$; the only possible components are $R_{0101}$ and its three skew variants. No pair-exchange identity is used.

(The base volume form is parallel.) Set $\varepsilon_{01}=\lambda$, $\varepsilon_{10}=-\lambda$, $\varepsilon_{00}=\varepsilon_{11}=0$, where $\lambda:=\sqrt{-D_q}>0$. By [L5], $\partial_C\lambda=\lambda(\Gamma^0{}_{C0}+\Gamma^1{}_{C1})$. The coordinate formula for the covariant derivative of a covariant two-tensor gives $\nabla_C\varepsilon_{AB}=\partial_C\varepsilon_{AB}-\Gamma^D{}_{CA}\varepsilon_{DB}-\Gamma^D{}_{CB}\varepsilon_{AD}$. For $(A,B)=(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ the two connection terms cancel because the only nonzero entries of $\varepsilon$ are opposite; for $(A,B)=(0,1)$ the value is $\partial_C\lambda-\Gamma^0{}_{C0}\lambda-\Gamma^1{}_{C1}\lambda=0$, and for $(A,B)=(1,0)$ it is the negative of this. Thus $\nabla_C\varepsilon_{AB}=0$ for every choice of indices.

(Pure trace.) By step 1.1 the only possibly nonzero lowered components are $R_{0101}$, $R_{0110}=-R_{0101}$, $R_{1001}=-R_{0101}$ and $R_{1010}=R_{0101}$; write $\rho:=R_{0101}$. In the sums $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}=\sum_{A,C}q^{AC}R_{ABCD}$ every term has an index repeated inside a pair except those with $\{A,B\}=\{C,D\}=\{0,1\}$, so $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{00}=q^{11}R_{1010}=q^{11}\rho$, $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{11}=q^{00}R_{0101}=q^{00}\rho$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{01}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{10}=q^{10}R_{1001}=-q^{01}\rho$. Cramer's rule [L2] gives $q^{00}q^{11}-(q^{01})^2=1/D_q$, hence $S_q=q^{00}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{00}+2q^{01}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{01}+q^{11}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{11}=\rho(2q^{00}q^{11}-2(q^{01})^2)=2\rho/D_q$. Therefore $\tfrac12S_q\,q_{00}=\rho q_{00}/D_q=\rho q^{11}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{00}$ by [L2], $\tfrac12S_q\,q_{11}=\rho q_{11}/D_q=\rho q^{00}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{11}$, and $\tfrac12S_q\,q_{01}=\rho q_{01}/D_q=-\rho q^{01}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{01}$; this proves (a).

(Hessian reduction.) Substituting $\operatorname{Ric}(q)=\tfrac12S_q\,q$ of step 2.1 into the first warped vacuum equation gives $\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r=\tfrac{rS_q}{4}q_{AB}$; tracing with $q^{AB}$ and using symmetry gives $\Delta_qr=\tfrac{rS_q}{4}\cdot2=\tfrac{rS_q}{2}$, hence $S_q=2\Delta_qr/r$ and $\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r=\tfrac12\Delta_qr\,q_{AB}$. The second warped vacuum equation gives $r\Delta_qr=1-z$ and hence $\Delta_qr=(1-z)/r$ and $S_q=2(1-z)/r^2$. This proves (b).

(Derivative of $z$.) Differentiating $q^{AE}q_{EB}=\delta^A{}_B$ and using the compatibility identity of [L1] gives [step 3.1, L1, L2, L3, algebra]
$$\partial_Cq^{AB}=-\Gamma^B{}_{CD}q^{AD}-\Gamma^A{}_{CD}q^{DB}.$$
Differentiate $z=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\,\partial_Br$ and substitute this identity. The two connection sums are equal after exchanging the dummy indices $A,B$, so
$$\partial_Cz=2\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\bigl(\partial_C\partial_Br-\sum_D\Gamma^D{}_{CB}\partial_Dr\bigr)=2\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\operatorname{Hess}_{CB}r.$$
By step 3.1, $\operatorname{Hess}_{CB}r=\tfrac12\Delta_qr\,q_{CB}$, so $\partial_Cz=\Delta_qr\,\partial_Cr=\tfrac{1-z}{r}\partial_Cr$. Hence $\partial_C(r(1-z))=(1-z)\partial_Cr-r\partial_Cz=0$ for $C=0,1$; since $V$ is connected and open and $r(1-z)$ is smooth, [L3] makes it constant, and writing this constant as $s$ gives $z=1-s/r$ because $r>0$. This proves (c).

(The Killing field.) By step 1.2, $

(Conclusion.) Step 1.1 supplies the pair antisymmetries, step 2.1 the pure trace (a), step 3.1 the reduction (b), step 4.1 the constancy (c), and step 4.2 the Killing field with its properties (d)-(e); clause (f) records the exact hypotheses, in particular that only the two displayed components of the four-dimensional vacuum equations, the positivity of $r$ and $z\ne0$ were used, and that the constant $s$ is produced on the connected set $V$.

boundaries.evidence: the identities are stated for the index sums over {0,1} and the fields K_A=sum_B epsilon_{AB} partial^B r; the sum has exactly two terms and step 4.1 evaluates them, so the two-element index family is checked rather than vacuous.

boundaries.reason: The proof divides by r>0, by the base dimension 2 in the trace identity, and by the field lambda=sqrt(-det q)>0; none of these denominators can vanish under the stated hypotheses.
The base is fixed at two dimensions because the pure-trace identity Ric(q)=S_q q/2 is special to that dimension; no one-dimensional variant is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 defines the lowered curvature with the factor lambda=sqrt(-Delta_q), positive by the hypothesis Delta_q<0, and the trace identity of step 2.1 uses the invertible q^{AB}; the degenerate case det q=0 is excluded by hypothesis and used nowhere.

boundaries.reason: V is an open connected set and no boundary point is evaluated; the constancy of s is asserted on V itself and the scope clause records that on a larger region it requires connectedness.
The volume form epsilon and the field K_A are defined by explicit formulas from the given orientation; no selection from a family of nonempty sets occurs.
The clauses derive necessary identities from the two vacuum equations; no biconditional is asserted.
The item does not claim that every solution of the reduced two-dimensional equations comes from a warped vacuum metric.

citations.quote:
Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty open set with global coordinates
$y=(y^0,y^1)$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]),
let $(q_{AB})$ be a smooth symmetric $2\times2$ matrix of functions on $V$
with

$$\Delta_q(y):=\det\bigl(q_{AB}(y)\bigr)<0\qquad(y\in V),$$

so that $q$ is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $V$ whose value
at every point is nondegenerate with inertia $(1,1,0)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]
clause (a), [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ be
a smooth function. Indices $A,B,C,D$ run over $\{0,1\}$ and indices
$i,j,k,l$ over the sphere directions below. Define on $V$:

$$(q^{AB}):=(q_{AB})^{-1},\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\tfrac12\sum_Dq^{AD}\bigl(\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}\bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r:=\partial_A\partial_Br-\sum_C\Gamma^C{}_{AB}\,\partial_Cr, \qquad \Delta_qr:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad z:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\,\partial_Br .$$

Further define

$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\sum_E\bigl(\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}\bigr), \qquad R_{ABCD}:=\sum_Eq_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD},$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=\sum_{A,C}q^{AC}R_{ABCD},\qquad S_q:=\sum_{B,D}q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}.$$

Let $S^2:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean
sphere with its induced smooth structure and round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]],
[[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]), let
$M:=V\times S^2$ carry the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
and let $\pi:M\to V$ and $\iota:M\to S^2$ be the projections. Define the
global symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$g:=\pi^*q+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$$

on $M$, where $r$ in this formula is pulled back from $V$. In any product
chart $(y^0,y^1,\xi^2,\xi^3)$, let $\gamma_{ij}$ be the round-metric
components of the angular chart. The components of $g$ are

$$g_{AB}:=q_{AB},\qquad g_{Ai}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=r^2\,\gamma_{ij} \qquad(A,B\in\{0,1\},\ i,j\in\{2,3\}),$$

Then:

**(a) The metric.** The global pullback formula defines a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$; at every point it is nondegenerate
with inertia $(3,1,0)$, so
$(M,g)$ is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(b) Christoffel symbols.** Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection of
$g$, unique by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]
clause (b) ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), and let
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}$ be its Christoffel symbols in a product chart. Then
the only nonzero symbols, beyond the displayed lower-index symmetry
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}=\Gamma^\mu{}_{\rho\nu}$, are

$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}\ \text{of the first display},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{Aj}=\frac{\partial_Ar}{r}\,\delta^i{}_j,\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-r\,q^{AB}\partial_Br\,\gamma_{ij},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{jk}\ \text{the round-sphere symbols in the chosen chart},$$

In a spherical-polar chart these are $\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$
and $\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, with all other
$\Gamma^i{}_{jk}$ vanishing. Pole charts use their own round-metric symbols.

**(c) Ricci tensor.** With $\operatorname{Ric}$ the Ricci tensor of $\nabla$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (c)), in every product
chart

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}-\frac{2}{r}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{Ai}=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=\bigl(1-z-r\Delta_qr\bigr)\gamma_{ij}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The statements are identities of the displayed component
functions in product charts and use no field equation, no vacuum condition and
no sign or positivity assumption on $s$; nothing is asserted about
completeness, geodesics, extensions or the physical reading of the coordinates.
The hypothesis $\Delta_q<0$ is used for nondegeneracy and inertia of $g$; it is
the only signature input.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and let $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$ be a family
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor at $p$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Suppose that the component
functions of $A$ are $C^\infty$ in the charts of one smooth atlas of $M$. Let
$(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be overlapping smooth charts of the maximal smooth atlas and
let $A_{cd}$ and $A'_{ab}$ denote their coordinate representatives in the
charts $x$ and $y$ as specified in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]].
For $q\in U\cap V$ put $u=y(q)$ and write $x(u):=(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$. Then

$$A'_{ab}(u) = \sum_{c,d\in I_n}\frac{\partial x^c}{\partial y^a}(u)\,\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial y^b}(u)\,A_{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),$$

where $\partial x^c/\partial y^a$ are the entries of the total derivative
$D(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$; $I_n$ is the label set of the supplier,
so in dimension four the sum runs from $0$ through $3$. In particular $A$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
on $M$: its components are $C^\infty$ in every chart of the maximal smooth
atlas.

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a connected nonempty open set, let $(q_{AB})$ be a
smooth symmetric matrix of functions on $V$ with $D_q:=\det(q_{AB})<0$
everywhere, and let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth; let
$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}$, $\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r$, $\Delta_qr$, $z$, $R^A{}_{BCD}$,
$R_{ABCD}$, $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}$ and $S_q$ be the functions defined in
the statement of [[lem-gr-warped-spherical-christoffel-and-ricci]], so that all
index sums run over $\{0,1\}$. Assume in addition that $z\ne0$ everywhere on
$V$ and that the **warped vacuum equations**

$$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}=\frac{2}{r}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad 1-z-r\Delta_qr=0 \qquad\text{on }V$$

hold, where the left-hand equation is the vanishing of the components
$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}$ and the right-hand equation the vanishing of the
components $\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}$ of the warped metric of
[[lem-gr-warped-spherical-christoffel-and-ricci]] clause (c) (the mixed
components vanish there identically). Define the **base volume form** by

$$\varepsilon_{AB}:=\sqrt{-D_q}\,\eta_{AB},\qquad \eta_{01}:=1,\quad\eta_{10}:=-1,\quad\eta_{00}:=\eta_{11}:=0,$$

and the **volume-form field** by

$$K_A:=\sum_B\varepsilon_{AB}\,\partial^Br,\qquad \partial^Br:=\sum_Cq^{BC}\partial_Cr,\qquad K^A:=\sum_Bq^{AB}K_B .$$

Then:

**(a) Pure trace in two dimensions.**
$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}=\tfrac12S_q\,q_{AB}$ and $S_q=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}$
on all of $V$.

**(b) Vacuum reduction of the Hessian.** $\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r=\tfrac12\Delta_qr\,q_{AB}$,
$\Delta_qr=\dfrac{1-z}{r}$ and $S_q=\dfrac{2\Delta_qr}{r}=\dfrac{2(1-z)}{r^2}$ on $V$.

**(c) Constancy of the mass parameter.** $\partial_Cz=\dfrac{1-z}{r}\,\partial_Cr$ for
$C=0,1$, hence $\partial_C\bigl(r(1-z)\bigr)=0$; consequently there is a
constant $s\in\mathbb R$ with

$$r(1-z)=s,\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad z=1-\frac{s}{r}\qquad\text{on }V .$$

**(d) The extra Killing field.** $K(r)=0$, $\sum_A K^A\partial_Ar=0$,
$\sum_{A,B}K^Aq_{AB}K^B=-z$, the field is nonzero at every point,
$\nabla_AK_B+\nabla_BK_A=0$ for the base connection $\Gamma^A{}_{BC}$ (so $K$
is a Killing field of $q$ in the sense of [[def-gr-killing-field]]), and the
fields $K$ and $\nabla r$ are pointwise linearly independent: the equalities
$\sum_A K^A\partial_Ar=0$, $\sum_{A,B}K^Aq_{AB}K^B=-z$ and
$\sum_{A,B}\partial_Ar\,q^{AB}\partial_Br=z\ne0$ show that neither field
vanishes and that the two are not proportional.

**(e) Explicit components of the Killing field.** With
$\lambda:=\sqrt{-D_q}>0$ one has $K^0=-\dfrac{\partial_1r}{\lambda}$ and
$K^1=\dfrac{\partial_0r}{\lambda}$.

**(f) Scope.** The statements are identities of the displayed functions and
use only the two warped vacuum equations, the strict positivity of $r$ and the
hypothesis $z\ne0$; no field equation of the four-dimensional metric beyond
those two components, no global hypothesis on $V$ and no sign or physical
reading of $s$ is assumed. The constant $s$ is determined on the connected
set $V$; that it is the same constant for a larger region requires that region
to be connected as well.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$, and let $p\in M$ satisfy $X_p\neq 0$.
Then there are local coordinates $(u^1,\dots,u^n)$ near $p$ in which

$$ X=\frac{\partial}{\partial u^1}. $$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: (Vacuum equations in warped form.) By [L1] the components of $\operatorname{Ric}(g)$ in a product chart are those displayed in the statement; the vacuum condition therefore gives $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}=(2/r)\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r$ and $1-z-r\Delta_qr=0$ on $V$, since $\gamma_{ij}$ is a nondegenerate matrix and $r>0$.

(The constant $s$.) The hypotheses of [[lem-gr-warped-base-vacuum-reduction]] are exactly the connectedness of $V$, $D_q<0$, $r>0$, $z\ne0$ and the two equations of step 1.1, so its clause (c) gives a constant $s\in\mathbb R$ with $r(1-z)=s$, that is, $z=1-s/r$; this is (a).

(Coordinates adapted to $K$.) By [L2] and step 2.1, $K$ is a nonvanishing smooth field on $V$, so by [L3] there are coordinates $(u^1,u^2)$ on a neighborhood of $p$ with $K=\partial_{u^1}$, and by $K(r)=0$ of [L2] the function $r$ is independent of $u^1$ there, so $r=r(u^2)$ with $\partial r/\partial u^2
e0$ because $
abla r
e0$; therefore $(T,r):=(u^1,r)$ is a smooth coordinate system on some open neighborhood $W$ of $p$ by [L4] and [L5], and $\partial_T=K$ there.

(The base metric in coordinates adapted to $K$.) In the coordinates $(T,r)$ from step 3.1, $K=\partial_T$ and $q_{TT}=q(K,K)=-z$ by [L2]. Since $K$ is Killing, $\mathcal L_{\partial_T}q=0$, so the coordinate components $q_{TT},q_{Tr},q_{rr}$ are independent of $T$. After shrinking $W$ to a coordinate rectangle, write $E(r)=q_{TT}$ and $F(r)=q_{Tr}$. The assumption $z\ne0$ gives $E=-z\ne0$. Define locally
$$H(r):=\int_{r_0}^{r}\frac{F(u)}{E(u)}\,du.$$
The integrand is smooth, and the first fundamental theorem of calculus gives $H'=F/E$. Replace the time coordinate by $\widehat T=T+H(r)$, leaving $r$ fixed; because the old coordinate is $T=\widehat T-H(r)$, the new cross coefficient is $F-EH'=0$, while $\partial_{\widehat T}=\partial_T=K$ and $q_{\widehat T\widehat T}=E=-z$. In these diagonal coordinates $z=q^{rr}=1/q_{rr}$ by its definition, so $q_{rr}=1/z$. Substituting $z=1-s/r$ from step 2.1 gives $q=-(1-\tfrac{s}{r})d\widehat T\otimes d\widehat T+(1-\tfrac{s}{r})^{-1}dr\otimes dr$. Renaming $\widehat T$ as $T$ proves (b).

(The metric and the Killing field.) In the product chart $(T,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ the components of $g$ are $g_{TT}=q_{TT}$, $g_{rr}=q_{rr}$, $g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all mixed components zero, by the definition of $g$ in [[lem-gr-warped-spherical-christoffel-and-ricci]]; substituting step 4.1 gives (c). Every displayed component is independent of $T$, and $\partial_T$ has components $(1,0,0,0)$ in this chart, so the Lie derivative $\mathcal L_{\partial_T}g$ has all components $\partial_Tg_{ab}=0$ and vanishes; by [L2] we also know $K$ is a Killing field of $q$ with $K(r)=0$ and $q(K,K)=-z$, and $\partial_T=K$ by step 3.1, so $\partial_T(r)=0$ and $g(\partial_T,\partial_T)=-z=-(1-s/r)$. This proves (d).

(Conclusion.) Step 2.1 proves (a), step 4.1 proves (b), step 5.1 proves (c) and (d); clause (e) records the local scope, the role of the hypotheses and the fact that $s$ is constant only on the connected set $V$.

boundaries.evidence: the statement quantifies over the index sums of the warped base and over the vacuum components, and step 1.1 evaluates the components Ric_AB and Ric_ij; the family of components is a fixed finite set and the case analysis is exhaustive, so no vacuous-quantification case remains.

The Statement assumes r>0 and z nonzero everywhere. In step 4.1, E(r)=q_TT=-z, so E(r) is nonzero on the whole shrunken coordinate rectangle and F/E is smooth. Only after removing the cross term is q_rr=1/z inferred. Points with r=s, where z=0, are excluded; the Remarks explicitly allow r to vary across that excluded level in a larger horizon-crossing chart.

boundaries.reason: Both the connected base V and the two-sphere factor are essential to the statement; no one-orbit or one-dimensional reduction is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 4.1 puts the base in the coordinates (T,r) where the metric coefficient is 1/z, finite because z != 0, and step 5.1 writes g with the sphere factor r^2 gamma; nondegeneracy follows from z != 0 and r>0, so the degenerate case is excluded by the hypotheses.

the statement is local: step 3.1 produces a neighborhood W of each point p, and the scope clause records that no endpoint of V and no asymptotic or global boundary is evaluated; the boundary value r=|s| where z or 1/z change sign is inside the chart and is not excluded by the local statement.

step 3.1 invokes the flow-box theorem to choose a coordinate T along K on a neighborhood of each point; the existence of that neighborhood is part of the theorem and the construction is explicit from the given field, so the choice is of a chart, made once per point and recorded, not of an element of an arbitrary family.

boundaries.reason: The clause (a) implication from vanishing Ricci to z=1-s/r is a one-way derivation, not the forward direction of a proclaimed equivalence.
The theorem does not claim that every metric with z=1-s/r and the displayed form is vacuum; no converse is asserted.

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework the
following statements.

**(i) Spacetime model.** The spacetime of a model of the framework is a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ as in
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: a smooth four-manifold $M$ without
boundary, a Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-manifold]]), and a time orientation $N$. Its points represent
idealized physical events; the vector $N$ fixes which causal directions are
future-directed; and the causal classification of tangent vectors along any
worldline is the classification of the Lorentz vector spaces $(T_pM,g_p)$
together with the future/past convention of the time orientation. The metric
$g$ is the gravitational field of the model: it is the object that the field
law of the framework constrains, and the curvature $R^g$ of the uniquely constructed torsion-free
$g$-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ of
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] is the model's representation of
gravity. That supplier defines $R^g(X,Y)Z=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z$
and proves the connection exists; this clause adds no independent connection
field. The rules by which ideal clocks, test bodies and
light rays couple to $g$ are adopted separately as physical assumptions of the
framework.

**(ii) Classical domain.** Geometry and matter are treated as classical
continuum fields: the model describes macroscopic configurations of matter and
a classical metric, with no quantum description of either. The framework makes
no claim that a real spacetime is exactly such a manifold, that matter is
exactly a classical continuum, or that the smooth description applies to
arbitrarily small scales or arbitrarily strong fields; those are domain
limitations of the model family, not consequences of it.

**(iii) Unity of the model.** A model of the framework is specified by its
geometry $(M,g,N)$ together with its matter content and the field law adopted
for it; the geometry alone selects no matter configuration and no dynamics
(the matter assumptions are
adopted separately, in the companion postulate on matter content). Physical
parameters enter through
the unit conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]; no
numerical value of a constant is asserted here.

**(iv) Smooth-branch restriction.** The fields of a model are defined on an
open domain of $M$; the metric is $C^\infty$ on all of $M$ and $M$ has no
boundary. Configurations in which a field fails to be smooth on a nonempty open
set, in which matter is concentrated on a lower-dimensional set in a way that
produces a distributional stress-energy tensor, or in which $M$ carries a
boundary, are outside the stated smooth domain of the framework and require
mathematics not supplied by these postulates.

**(v) Status.** These are adopted assumptions. They are not derived from the
mathematics of manifolds, from any symmetry principle, or from experiment; the
equivalence principle and covariance arguments motivate but do not prove them.
Testing the framework means comparing predictions computed from a fully
specified model — geometry, matter content and field law — with observations,
and agreement is evidence about the model, not a proof of these postulates.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]], the following statements
about the matter content of a model.

**(i) Matter content is model input.** A model of the framework specifies its
nongravitational fields or matter and their explicit equations of motion and
couplings. The geometric data $(M,g,N)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and covariance of the model's equations
under relabelling of events do not select those fields, equations or couplings:
different matter specifications over the same geometry are different models of
the framework, and no dynamical selection principle is asserted.

**(ii) Smooth matter and its stress-energy tensor.** The matter of a model on
its matter domain is represented by smooth fields on an open domain
$U\subseteq M$, and the model's stress-energy tensor is the smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $T$ on $U$ of
[[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]], with the unit reading recorded there.
The relation of $T$ to the matter fields is part of the model: a model derived
from an action defines $T$ as the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of that action,
while a model that prescribes $T$ directly is a separate source model.

**(iii) Consistency with the field law.** Where a model prescribes $T$
independently of matter fields, the prescription is admissible only if it meets
the consistency conditions imposed by the gravitational field law adopted for
the model, stated where that law is stated; in the action formulation the
matter equations, their coupling to the metric, and the on-shell conservation
of $T$ are derived within the model rather than assumed. Conservation is an
on-shell statement about a specified model and is not automatic for an
arbitrary smooth symmetric $T$.

**(iv) Energy conditions are optional additional assumptions.** A model may
adopt any of the pointwise inequalities of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]] as
further assumptions on its stress-energy tensor. None of them is a consequence
of the preceding clauses, of the field law, or of the symmetry of $T$; each
model records which conditions, if any, it adopts, and a model that adopts none
is not thereby excluded.

**(v) Scope and exclusions.** Idealizations such as unmodeled self-force,
finite-size and tidal corrections, dispersion, dissipation, and quantum effects
are outside the framework unless the model's explicit equations include them;
matter concentrated in a distributional or lower-dimensional source, and
matter configurations whose fields fail to be smooth on the model domain, are
outside the stated smooth branch and require additional mathematics. The
adoption of a matter model is not a claim that it describes nature.

Adopt as the field law of the direct-equation presentation of the classical
gravitational framework, for models satisfying
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]], the following statement.

**(i) The equation.** Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12Sg_{ab}$ be the Einstein tensor of that
connection ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Let
$T$ be the model's stress-energy tensor field on its matter domain
$U\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]) and let
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a constant parameter with dimension
$\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $G_N>0$, $c>0$ the constants of
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Adopt

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\,T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U$$

as the field law of the model. Writing
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ and $T_{ab}=g_{ac}g_{bd}T^{cd}$ for the lowered tensor,
the equation reads $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$

**(ii) Matter content.** The equation constrains the metric and the matter of
the model jointly. A model specifies its matter sector as in
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]: a scalar-field model with its action
and stress-energy tensor ([[def-gr-scalar-field-matter-model]]), or a dust or perfect-fluid model with prescribed
stress-energy tensor and matter equations. The consistency condition that
every solution must satisfy, $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$, is not adopted separately; it
is a consequence of the equation and of the contracted second Bianchi identity
and is derived in [[pthm-gr-einstein-consistency-and-energy-conditions]].

**(iii) Alternative presentation.** The action formulation of the same field
law is adopted separately in [[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]]. A
model adopts exactly one of the two presentations. They are alternative
presentations of one classical field law: the action-to-equation theorem of
this page identifies the equation obtained from stationarity of the total
action with the equation displayed in clause (i), and the direct presentation
is not an additional premise of an action-formulated model.

**(iv) Status and scope.** The equation is an adopted law of the model. It is
not derived from mathematical symmetry, from the equivalence principle, or
from observation; covariance and correspondence arguments motivate but do not
prove it. No numerical value of $c$, $G_N$ or $\Lambda$ is asserted, and no
claim is made that any particular metric or matter configuration solves the
equation or describes nature. The smooth-branch exclusions of
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] apply: distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, boundaries with junction conditions, and non-smooth
fields are outside this formulation. Comparisons of a model's predictions with
data test the combined model — geometry, matter content and this law — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of the postulate.

This item fixes the unit and coordinate readings of the explicitly defined
Lorentzian objects, smooth-curve proper time and four-velocity of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], the tensor fields of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and the constructed connection,
curvature, Ricci and scalar fields of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]].
It states conventions, not a physical law or a measurement.

**(a) Constants and tensor slot.** Adopt $c>0$ with SI dimension
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, $G_N>0$ with dimension
$\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm s^{-2}$, and a signed parameter
$\Lambda$ with dimension $\mathrm m^{-2}$. No numerical value is asserted.
Define $\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$, of dimension
$\mathrm m^{-1}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm s^2$.
For a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $T$ adopt the convention that its
components $T_{AB}=T(e_A,e_B)$ in an ordered $g$-orthonormal basis are energy
per volume, $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$.
This is a tensor slot and unit convention; interpreting a particular $T$ as
matter is a subsequent definition. Therefore $\kappa T_{AB}$ has dimension
$\mathrm m^{-2}$. No positivity, conservation or matter realization is assumed.

**(b) Coordinates and dimensions.** In a length-coordinate chart,
$x^0=ct$ and all four coordinates have units $\mathrm m$; $g_{ab}$ are
dimensionless and the quadratic line element $ds^2=g_{ab}dx^adx^b$ has units
$\mathrm m^2$. The Christoffel symbols defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) have units
$\mathrm m^{-1}$: the constructed formula differentiates dimensionless
$g_{ab}$ once with respect to a length coordinate. Curvature components have
units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ since the curvature operator differentiates the
connection once more and includes products of two connection coefficients;
so do $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ and scalar curvature $S$ in these coordinates.
In a time-coordinate chart $x^0=t$ has units $\mathrm s$, and $g_{00}$ has
units $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$; mixed, spatial, angular or other chart
components have the dimensions obtained by the coordinate Jacobians. A single
component has no universal dimension in a general chart. Orthonormal-frame
readings use the normalized geometric basis, with its length normalization.

**(c) Curves and invariant readings.** For the smooth future timelike curve
and positive scaling parameter of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] (e),
read $c$ as in (a) and
$\tau(s)=\tau_0+c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}\,dr$
as a proper-time parameter in seconds. Its four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$
has length-coordinate and normalized orthonormal components in
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$; in a time-coordinate chart $U^0=dt/d\tau$
is dimensionless and other component dimensions follow the coordinates.
Lorentzian length $c\,\Delta\tau$ is in metres. The tensors $R^g$,
$\operatorname{Ric}$ and the scalar $S$ have the orthonormal readings
$\mathrm m^{-2}$, whereas the lowered curvature components in a mixed chart
have the units required by the metric and coordinate slots.

**(d) Future observer readings and SI restoration.** Let $n$ be a future
unit timelike vector, $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)<0$. Define
$\rho_n:=T(n,n)$, $j_n:=-\sharp(T(n,\cdot))$ and its spatial part
$\phi_n:=j_n-\rho_n n$; indeed $g(j_n,n)=-\rho_n$, so
