$g(\phi_n,n)=0$. In a $g$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n$, set
$\phi^i=-T(e_0,e_i)=T^{0i}$ for $i=1,2,3$. The **SI energy flux** vector
and **SI momentum density** covector are, respectively,

$$q_n:=c\phi_n,\qquad p_n:=\phi_n^{\flat}/c,\qquad q_n^i=-cT_{0i},\qquad (p_n)_i=-T_{0i}/c.$$

Thus $\rho_n$ and each $\phi^i$ have units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$;
$q_n^i$ has units $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $(p_n)_i$ has units
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$. Stress components $T_{ij}$ have
units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{Pa}$. Tensor components retain the
common energy-density units; the factors of $c$ convert their mixed readings
to different SI quantities. Future-directedness and the signs here are part
of the convention, not positivity assumptions on $T$.

**(e) Natural units.** Setting $c=1$, or additionally $G_N=1$, abbreviates
these dimensionful conventions. Restore the factors displayed above before
comparison with SI quantities; in particular the same spatial tensor component
corresponds to energy flux multiplied by $c$ and momentum density divided by
$c$. A length-coordinate null ray obeys $|d\mathbf x/dx^0|=1$ in an inertial
flat chart; this coordinate relation does not change the physical constant.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and the matter-content
assumptions of the framework, the following rules by which ideal clocks, test
bodies and light couple to the metric $g$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** An **ideal clock** is an idealized physical device
carried along a future timelike worldline ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]])
whose readings are assumed to reproduce the proper time of that worldline:
the difference of two readings taken at two events of the worldline is the
proper-time increment between those events as defined by the metric, and it is
independent of the construction of the clock. Two ideal clocks moving along
the same worldline differ only by an additive constant (their choice of zero);
different worldlines generally accrue different proper times between the same
pair of events. The physical constant $c$ and the unit of duration are those
of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(ii) Free fall of massive test bodies.** A **test body** is an uncharged
idealized body whose internal structure is small compared with the scale over
which the geometry of the model varies and whose gravitational self-field is
negligible within the model. An **ideal freely falling massive test body** is
assumed to have a worldline that is a future timelike geodesic of the
metric-selected connection ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), traversed with physical
four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfying
$g_{\gamma(\tau)}(U,U)=-c^2$; proper time is an affine parameter of the
worldline ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The
worldline is determined by the event at which the body is released together
with its four-velocity there, by the uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value
problem ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]); no force, charge, or
rest mass of the body enters this rule.

**(iii) Light rays.** In the geometric-optics approximation an **ideal light
ray** propagating in the model is assumed to be a future null geodesic of the
metric-selected connection
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]). A null worldline carries no proper
time and no four-velocity in the sense of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]; within the approximation the
propagation of an ideal ray is independent of its frequency, and only the
ray's direction in the tangent space is fixed, not a scale along it.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The three rules are adopted in the test-field
regime of the smooth classical model: the clocks, bodies and rays do not
back-react on the geometry, and the geometry varies smoothly on the scales
relevant to them. Configurations requiring the body's own gravitational field,
radiation reaction, an electromagnetic or other self-force, finite-size or
tidal couplings beyond the test-body idealization, non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion or dissipation of light, or quantum effects are
outside these assumptions and require additional model content. The
assumptions do not assert that any real clock, body or light ray is exactly
ideal, nor do they attach measured readings to any model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For $a<c<b$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(c)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(c)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and curvature data $R^a{}_{bcd}$, $R_{abcd}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$, $G_{ab}$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In every spherical-polar
product chart
$(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$, writing $f'=\frac{df}{dr}=s/r^2$ and
$f''=\frac{d^2f}{dr^2}=-2s/r^3$:

**(a) Curvature components.** All nonzero components of the lowered
curvature tensor, up to the symmetries of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$R_{0101}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad R_{0202}=\frac{rf f'}{2},\qquad R_{0303}=\frac{rf f'\sin^2\vartheta}{2},$$

$$R_{1212}=-\frac{rf'}{2f},\qquad R_{1313}=-\frac{rf'\sin^2\vartheta}{2f},\qquad R_{2323}=r^2\bigl(1-f\bigr)\sin^2\vartheta .$$

Every component whose index pairs do not coincide as unordered pairs, and
every component with an index repeated inside a pair, vanishes.

**(b) Ricci tensor.** The Ricci tensor has the diagonal components

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=f\Bigl(\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}\Bigr),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{11}=-\frac{1}{f}\Bigl(\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}\Bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{22}=1-f-rf',\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{33}=\bigl(1-f-rf'\bigr)\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and all mixed components $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ with $a\ne b$ vanish.

**(c) Vanishing for the model.** For $f(r)=1-s/r$ one has
$\frac{f''}{2}+\frac{f'}{r}=0$ and $1-f-rf'=0$; consequently

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=0,\qquad S=0,\qquad G_{ab}=0$$

on the regular angular locus and, as tensor identities, on all of $M$ by
smoothness and density. In particular the
Schwarzschild exterior metric is a Ricci-flat metric, and $G=0$ holds as an
identity of smooth tensor fields.

**(d) The curvature does not vanish.** The model is not locally flat. The
global base-field contraction $R_{0101}:=g(R(\partial_0,\partial_r)
\partial_r,\partial_0)$ equals $-s/r^3$ on the regular angular locus, hence
everywhere by smoothness and density. It is therefore nowhere zero even
though the Ricci and Einstein tensors vanish identically.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Define the
smooth vector field

$$n:=f^{-1/2}\,\partial_0=\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1/2}\partial_0$$

on $M$. Then:

**(a) Observer congruence.** $n$ is a smooth observer congruence on $M$ in the
sense of [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]: $g(n,n)=-1$ and
$g(n,N)<0$ at every point, so $n$ is a future-directed unit timelike field.

**(b) Integral curves.** For any $p=(c_0,r_0,\omega_0)\in M$, including sphere poles, the maximal integral curve of $n$ through $p$, with length-valued flow parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, is
$$\lambda\mapsto\bigl(c_0+f(r_0)^{-1/2}\lambda,\ r_0,\ \omega_0\bigr).$$
It is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and is the **static observer worldline** at radius $r_0$. In a spherical-polar chart it has constant angular coordinates $(\vartheta_0,\varphi_0)$; in any angular chart the sphere point is constant, and the global coordinate $x^0$ increases monotonically.

**(c) Proper time and clock rate.** Along each static observer worldline the
proper time $\tau$ is an affine function of the flow parameter $\lambda$, with
$\frac{d\tau}{d\lambda}=\frac1c$, and

$$\Delta\tau=\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{c}\,\Delta x^0=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t,$$

where $\Delta x^0$ is the coordinate difference in metres between two events
of the worldline and $\Delta t=\Delta x^0/c$ is the same difference in
seconds. In particular the proper-time increment is strictly positive for
$\Delta x^0>0$, and it is smaller than $\Delta t$ at every finite radius
because $0<f(r_0)<1$.

**(d) Clock-rate ratio.** For two static observers at radii
$r_1,r_2\in(s,\infty)$ compared over the same coordinate interval
$\Delta x^0$, the proper-time increments satisfy

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_1}{\Delta\tau_2}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_1)}{f(r_2)}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-s/r_1}{1-s/r_2}} .$$

**(e) Acceleration.** The acceleration field of the congruence is
$a:=\nabla_nn=\frac{f'(r)}{2}\,\partial_1=\frac{s}{2r^2}\,\partial_r$; it is
spatial, nowhere zero, and points in the direction of increasing $r$, so the
static observers are not geodesics.

**(f) Scope.** These are identities of the geometric datum. The reading of
$\tau$ as the time measured by an ideal clock and of the congruence as a
family of static observers belongs to the framework's postulates and is not
asserted here; no measurement and no comparison with any observed rate is
made.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty
open subset, carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field
$n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that
$n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly,

$$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$

Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing. A single observer
at a point is therefore not a congruence, and a congruence is not an ordered
basis or frame of $T_qM$.

**(b) Observer curves.** Because $n$ is a smooth vector field on $U$, the
theorem on maximal integral curves
([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]) assigns to every $q\in U$ a unique
maximal integral curve $\gamma_q:I_q\to U$ of $n$ with $\gamma_q(0)=q$,
defined on an open interval $I_q\subseteq\mathbb R$. We call these curves the
**observers** (or **observer curves**) of the congruence. Each observer is
regular: $\gamma_q'(s)=n_{\gamma_q(s)}$ and $\lVert n\rVert_g=1$ at every
parameter value, so the tangent vector is unit timelike and future-directed at
every parameter value. Completeness of the maximal intervals $I_q$, and global
product or foliation structure of $U$, are not asserted. The parameter $s$ is
the flow parameter of $n$; it is not identified with any clock reading here.

**(c) Adapted charts.** An **$n$-adapted chart** is a smooth chart
$(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U'\to\mathbb R^4$ of $M$ whose domain $U'$ is a nonempty
open subset of $U$ and whose **spatial coordinates** $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant
along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U'$; equivalently, for every
$q\in U'$ the observer curve $\gamma_q$ satisfies
$u^i(\gamma_q(s))=u^i(q)$ for all $s$ with $\gamma_q(s)\in U'$ and
$i=1,2,3$. No global adapted chart, and no adapted chart on all of $U$, is
asserted by this definition; one exists near every point of $U$ by the
existence corollary proved on this page.

**(d) Scope.** A congruence is a field of observer directions on an open set; it
is not a chart, not a tetrad field, and not a family of parametrized
worldlines with specified domains. The physical reading of its observer curves
as ideal-clock worldlines, and the identification of the flow parameter with a
measurable time, belong to the physical postulates of the framework and are not
asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
$f'=s/r^2$. Then:

For arbitrary $x^0_0,\varphi_0\in\mathbb R$, put
$\omega_0=(\cos\varphi_0,\sin\varphi_0,0)\in S^2$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$
define the rotation
$$R_\alpha(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(y_1\cos\alpha-y_2\sin\alpha,\ y_1\sin\alpha+y_2\cos\alpha,\ y_3),$$
and the global axial vector field $\Phi(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(-y_2,y_1,0)$ on $S^2$;
it is tangent because $y\cdot\Phi(y)=0$ for $y\in S^2$.
In every spherical-polar chart near the equator, $\Phi=\partial_\varphi$;
longitude expressions below are local chart expressions for the global sphere
curve $R_\alpha\omega_0$.

**(a) Existence of circular timelike geodesics.** Let $r_0>3s/2$ and choose
$\ell\in\mathbb R$ with

$$\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}>0,\qquad e:=\Bigl(f(r_0)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2} =\frac{c(r_0-s)\sqrt 2}{\sqrt{r_0(2r_0-3s)}}>0 .$$

Then the globally defined curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ is

$$\gamma(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr).$$
In each local polar chart along it, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and the longitude is
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to a constant multiple of $2\pi$.

It is a future timelike geodesic of the datum, with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$
and with the conserved quantities $e=-g(\gamma',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\gamma',\Phi)$ of
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is an equatorial future timelike geodesic with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$ and its conserved angular momentum satisfies
$\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$; in particular there is no timelike
circular geodesic with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Define

$$R:(s/4,\infty)\to(s,\infty),\qquad R(\rho):=\rho\Bigl(1+\frac{s}{4\rho}\Bigr)^{2},$$

and define the **isotropic radius** of a point $p\in M$ by
$\rho(p):=\rho_0(r(p))$, where $\rho_0:(s,\infty)\to(s/4,\infty)$ is the
inverse of $R$. Write $a:=s/(4\rho)$. Then:

**(a) The coordinate change.** $R$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse
and $R'(\rho)=1-\frac{s^2}{16\rho^2}>0$; its inverse is the smooth function

$$\rho_0(r)=\frac{(r-\tfrac{s}{2})+\sqrt{r(r-s)}}{2},$$

and the identity $R(\rho)=\rho+\frac{s}{2}+\frac{s^2}{16\rho}$ holds on
$(s/4,\infty)$.

**(b) The metric in isotropic coordinates.** In the chart
$(x^0,\rho,\vartheta,\varphi)$ obtained by replacing the coordinate $r$ by
$\rho(p)$ (so that $r=R(\rho)$ in the chart), the metric of the datum has the
components

$$g=-\Bigl(\frac{1-a}{1+a}\Bigr)^2 d(x^0)^2+(1+a)^4\bigl(d\rho^2+\rho^2(d\vartheta^2+\sin^2\vartheta\,d\varphi^2)\bigr),$$

that is, $g_{00}=-(1-a)^2/(1+a)^2$, $g_{\rho\rho}=(1+a)^4$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=(1+a)^4\rho^2$,
$g_{\varphi\varphi}=(1+a)^4\rho^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all other components
zero.

**(c) Conformal flatness and the large-radius expansion.** On the region
where $(\rho,\vartheta,\varphi)$ are the standard spherical coordinates of
$\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, the spatial part of $g$ is the conformally flat
metric $(1+a)^4\,\delta$, with $\delta=d\rho^2+\rho^2(d\vartheta^2+\sin^2\vartheta\,d\varphi^2)$
in Cartesian coordinates $y=\rho\,\hat\omega$,
$\lvert y\rvert=\rho$. Moreover, for every lower bound $\rho_*>s/4$ there is
a constant $C(\rho_*)$ with

$$\Bigl|\bigl(1+\frac{s}{4\rho}\bigr)^4-1-\frac{s}{\rho}\Bigr|\le\frac{C(\rho_*)s^2}{\rho^2}\qquad\text{for }\rho\ge\rho_*,$$

and $\rho_0(r)=r-\frac{s}{2}-\frac{s^2}{16r}+O(s^3/r^2)$ as $r/s\to\infty$
with fixed $s>0$; in particular $\rho$ is
not equal to the areal radius $r$.

**(d) The comparison warning.** The areal-radius coefficient
$f(r)^{-1}=(1-s/r)^{-1}=1+s/r+O(r^{-2})$ and the isotropic coefficient
$(1+s/(4\rho))^4=1+s/\rho+O(\rho^{-2})$ agree at leading order but differ at
next order when one substitutes $\rho=r$; consequently any comparison of the
Schwarzschild coefficients with weak-field coefficients stated in another
chart must first convert to a single chart by the explicit map $R$ and must
carry the resulting error terms. Matching coefficient functions in two
different radial coordinates without the conversion is not a valid
identification.

Let $(M,g_\eta,N_\eta)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and constant components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be a
nonempty open spacetime region, identified with its image in $\mathbb R^4$,
and let $\pi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be the spatial projection
$\pi(x^0,\mathbf x)=\mathbf x$. Its image $U:=\pi(\Omega)$ is open: a
coordinate ball in $\Omega$ about any point projects onto a ball about that
point's spatial coordinates. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact. Let $c>0$ and
$G_N>0$ be the constants of the framework's conventions and put
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$. The coordinates have units of metres, $c$ has units
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, and $\varepsilon$ is dimensionless.

**(a) Structural data.** A tuple $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ is
**stationary weak-field data** when

- $L>0$ is a length, $C>0$ is dimensionless, and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is
  dimensionless;
- $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth dimensionless spatial function and
  $r=(r_{ab})$ is a family of smooth dimensionless spatial functions
  $r_{ab}:(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)\times U\to\mathbb R$ for some
  $\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon_0$
  ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]);
- for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi(\pi(p)))+r_{00}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&a=b=0,\\[2pt] r_{0i}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&\{a,b\}=\{0,i\},\\[2pt] (1-2\varepsilon\varphi(\pi(p)))\,\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&a=i,\ b=j,\end{cases}$$

  is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\varepsilon)$ on
  $\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
- **(spatial factorization and stationarity)** all metric components factor
  through $\pi$ by construction. Thus points of $\Omega$ with the same
  spatial coordinates have the same metric components, even when they lie in
  different connected components of that spatial fiber, and
  $\partial_0g_{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$;
- **(spatial bounds)** for every multiindex $\alpha\in\mathbb N^3$ with
  $|\alpha|\le2$ and every $\mathbf x\in K$,

$$|\partial^\alpha\varphi(\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{00}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|+|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{0i}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^{|\alpha|}}.$$

  (Derivatives are with respect to $x^1,x^2,x^3$; here $|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}|$
  is the maximum over $i,j$ and $|\partial^\alpha r_{0i}|$ is the maximum
  over $i$.)

**(b) Derived data.** For stationary weak-field data define the
**spatial potential**

$$\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a smooth spatial function of dimension $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ in the
framework's unit conventions; its pullback to $\Omega$ is stationary. The
symmetric component family $g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ is the **perturbation of the
family**.

**(c) Einstein families.** Stationary weak-field data form an **Einstein
family with coupling $\kappa$** when for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$
there is a smooth symmetric component field $T_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)$ on
$\Omega$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) satisfying

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection of
$g(\varepsilon)$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In that case define the
**spatial density read from the time-time component**

$$\rho_\varepsilon(\mathbf x):=\frac{T_{00}(\varepsilon,x^0,\mathbf x)}{c^2}\qquad\text{on }U,$$

where any $x^0$ with $(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\Omega$ may be used. This is
well-defined: the metric is the pullback of spatial functions, so its
coordinate curvature components, and hence $T_{00}=\kappa^{-1}G_{00}$, are
constant on each fiber of $\pi$, including when that fiber is disconnected.
It has units $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; it is a coordinate-component
density and is not thereby the dust rest-mass density.

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes a class of metric families and the vocabulary
of the weak-field bridge: the spatial factorization, component form,
stationarity, spatial derivative bounds, potential, and the equation that
upgrades the data to an Einstein family. It asserts that no family exists,
that $\partial_0$ is timelike or a Killing field, that the inverse metrics
are uniformly bounded or that $\rho_\varepsilon$ is positive; those are
consequences proved separately where they are used. The family is an explicit
input-family hypothesis: neither its existence for prescribed Newtonian
initial data nor its construction from other data is claimed. The physical
reading of the components, of $G_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$, of $\Phi$ and of
$\rho_\varepsilon$ belongs to the framework's postulates and unit
conventions, which are separate items.

This item defines the auxiliary framework used to formulate the Newtonian
bridge, and the dictionary by which the relativistic weak-field data are read
against it. It asserts no approximation; the approximation statement is a
separate theorem of this page.

**(a) Newtonian comparison model.** A **Newtonian comparison model** is a
tuple $(O,\Phi_N,\rho_N,G_{\mathrm{cmp}})$ consisting of

- a nonempty open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, the **spatial region**, whose
  points are read as positions in metres;
- a $C^\infty$ function $\Phi_N:O\to\mathbb R$, the **Newtonian potential**,
  whose values are read in $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$;
- a $C^\infty$ function $\rho_N:O\to\mathbb R$, the **Newtonian mass
  density**, whose values are read in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; and
- a real constant $G_{\mathrm{cmp}}>0$ with the dimension
  $\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$,

such that the **Newtonian field equation**

$$\Delta\Phi_N=4\pi G_{\mathrm{cmp}}\rho_N\qquad\text{on }O$$

holds, where $\Delta$ is the Laplacian on $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). A **comparison motion** of the model is
a $C^2$ curve $q:J\to O$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ whose points
are read as times in seconds, satisfying the **Newtonian equation of motion**

$$q''(t)=-\nabla\Phi_N\bigl(q(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J),$$

the gradient being the total derivative of $\Phi_N$
([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).
The model is an auxiliary classical model: its equations are adopted as part
of the definition of the comparison framework and are not derived here from
the relativistic framework or from anything else.

**(b) The correspondence identification.** Let
$(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data over
the spacetime region $\Omega$, with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$, parameters
$c>0$ and $G_N>0$, an Einstein family, spatial potential
$\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$, and coordinate density
$\rho_\varepsilon=T_{00}(\varepsilon)/c^2$ on $U$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]],
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]],
[[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]). A **comparison reading** consists of a
Newtonian comparison model $(O,\Phi_N,\rho_N,G_{\mathrm{cmp}})$ and the
following adopted dictionary:

1. the Newtonian spatial region is $O=U$, the spatial projection of $\Omega$,
   and chart spatial coordinates in metres are read as Newtonian positions;
2. chart time $t=x^0/c$ in seconds is read as the Newtonian time parameter;
3. the spatial potential $\Phi:U\to\mathbb R$ is identified exactly with
   $\Phi_N$, both with units $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$;
4. the constants $G_N$ and $G_{\mathrm{cmp}}$ are identified exactly.

The Newtonian source density $\rho_N$ continues to satisfy its exact model
equation in clause (a). It is not identified here with either
$\rho_\varepsilon=T_{00}/c^2$ or a dust rest-mass density; no density error
estimate is part of this definition.

**(c) Status.** The dictionary of (b) is an **adopted correspondence
assumption**: it fixes which regions, coordinates, potentials and couplings
of the two frameworks are to be compared, in which units, and is part of the
formulation of any bridge statement built on it. The Newtonian source density
$\rho_N$, the relativistic coordinate density $\rho_\varepsilon$ and a dust
rest-mass density are distinct quantities. Any error-qualified matching
between them is a separate theorem under its own hypotheses. This definition
neither asserts exact density equality nor agreement of the models, and it
does not assert that either framework describes nature.

**(d) Scope and exclusions.** The comparison model is smooth and
source-continuous: point masses and delta densities are excluded, no boundary
conditions at spatial infinity are imposed, and no statement is made about
the numerical value, sign convention or uncertainty of $G_N$, $G_{\mathrm{cmp}}$
or $c$; those belong to the framework's conventions and to empirical work
elsewhere. The comparison model has no relativistic content: it carries no
metric, no causal structure and no stress-energy tensor, and its
identification with the weak-field data is confined to the items listed in
(b).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Adopt one of the two presentations of the framework's field law, that is,
[[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]] or
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], for a model with geometric data and matter
sector satisfying [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
and curvature tensors $R^{a}{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$,
$G_{ab}$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let $T$ be the model's smooth
symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the matter domain
([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]), let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be the
constant parameter and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $U\subseteq M$ be the
model's open matter domain and suppose the field law holds on $U$,

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U .$$

**(a) Necessary conservation.** $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$. Consequently a
prescribed smooth symmetric $T$ with $\nabla^aT_{ab}\neq0$ at some point cannot
satisfy the field law there for any metric on which $T$ is smooth.

**(b) Trace.** On $U$, $g^{ab}T_{ab}$ satisfies
$-S+4\Lambda=\kappa\,g^{ab}T_{ab}$.

**(c) Parameter variation.** If instead $\Lambda:U\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth
function and the field law $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds on $U$
with that function in place of a constant, then on $U$

$$\kappa\nabla^aT_{ab}=\partial_b\Lambda .$$

Consequently, at every point where $d\Lambda\ne0$, the equation requires
$\nabla^aT_{ab}\ne0$; where $d\Lambda=0$, this identity imposes conservation.
A smooth $\Lambda$ can be locally constant but nonconstant across disconnected
components of $U$, in which case this identity does not force nonconservation.

**(d) A vacuum solution.** In the global vacuum example take
$U=M=\mathbb R^4$ with the identity chart and the flat metric
$g_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ (a smooth Lorentzian metric
with time orientation $N=\partial_0$), the field law with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$
holds: $G=0$ and $S=0$ for the flat metric. With $T=0$ and $\Lambda\neq0$ it
fails, since $G+\Lambda g=\Lambda g\neq0$.

**(e) Energy conditions are additional assumptions.** Neither adopted
presentation of the field law contains a clause imposing any of the weak, null,
dominant or strong energy conditions of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]]; each of
the four conditions is available to a model only as a further assumption in the
sense of clause (iv) of [[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]], and the field
law (a)-(d) derives none of them.

**(f) Perfect-fluid rest-frame reading.** Let $(\varepsilon,p,n,T)$ be a
perfect-fluid model on its matter domain
([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]), and at any $p\in U$ let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be a $g_p$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n_p$. Then
$T_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,p,p,p)$ in that basis, and at $p$

$$T\ \text{satisfies WEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies NEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+p\ge0,\qquad T\ \text{satisfies DEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge|p|,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies SEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+3p\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0 .$$

In particular a model with $\varepsilon>0$ and $p=-\varepsilon$ satisfies the
NEC, WEC and DEC and violates the SEC; the inequality signs here are those of
the strict-timelike convention of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]], under which
continuity extensions to the causal cone are not assumed.

derivations.claim: (The model and its field law.) By [L1] and [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] the datum is a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold without boundary, so it satisfies the spacetime postulate by [A1]; $T=0$ is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on the matter domain $M$. By [L1], $G_{ab}\equiv0$; with $\Lambda=0$ and $T=0$, $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=0=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds identically and $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ trivially, so the prescription is admissible by [A1] and satisfies the field law by [A2], which is the vacuum solution of [L4]. That the model is not locally flat is [L1]. This proves (a).

(Static clock readings.) By [L2] the integral curves of $n$ are the constant-radius worldlines and are smooth future timelike curves; by [A3] the model assigns to an ideal clock carried along each of them the reading equal to the proper time, and [L2] gives the increment $\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\Delta t$ and the ratio $\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$ for two radii. Since [L2] also gives $a=\frac{s}{2r^2}\partial_r\ne0$, the static worldlines are not geodesics, so by [A3] the model does not assign them to freely falling test bodies. This proves (b).

(The mass parameter.) By [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a) the parameter $m_*$ determines the datum only through $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and the unit conventions; by [L3] the coordinate angular velocity of a circular timelike geodesic of the datum at radius $r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$ satisfies $(d\varphi/dt)^2=G_Nm_*/r_0^3$. For the isotropic chart, the exact coefficient in [L3] gives
$$g_{00}+1=\frac{4a}{(1+a)^2}=4a+O(a^2)=+\frac{s}{\rho}+O(\rho^{-2})=+\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2\rho}+O(\rho^{-2}),\qquad a=\frac{s}{4\rho},$$
as $\rho\to\infty$ with fixed $s$, by the exact identity $(1+a)^{-2}=1+O(a)$. The weak-field convention and comparison dictionary in [L3] identify the leading coefficient as $-2\Phi_N/c^2$ for $\Phi_N(\rho)=-G_Nm_*/\rho$. The framework's unit conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]] read $m_*$ in kilograms, and these are the model's own occurrences of the parameter; no numerical value, source model or observation enters. This proves (c).

(Status and scope.) Steps 1.1-1.3 establish (a)-(c) as consequences of the adopted postulates and the cited mathematics, using no observation, apparatus or measured input; clause (d) records that the model is one solution among many, that the exterior domain excludes the horizon and interior and that no empirical claim is made.

boundaries.reason: The model is one explicit datum with one stress-energy prescription T=0; no family or union over an unbounded index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 verifies T=0 is admissible and G=0 holds with Lambda=0, so the vanishing fields themselves are the checked case; step 1.3 evaluates the far-field coefficient -s/rho and the circular-orbit law with r_0>3s/2 and rho>s/4, no denominator vanishing.

boundaries.reason: No one-parameter or unit-mass specialization is asserted; the model is stated with the general parameters c, G_N, m_*.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 uses the metric-properties lemma to record that the datum is a smooth nondegenerate time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, so the degenerate case is excluded before the field law is read; the non-flatness clause uses R_0101=-s/r^3 != 0.

boundaries.reason: The model domain is r>s and the boundary r=s is excluded by clause (d) of the scope; no endpoint value of the field law is evaluated.
The datum, the congruence and the constants are fixed by the adopted postulates; no choice from a nonempty family is made.
The theorem derives the field law and the clock law from the adopted postulates; no equivalence is asserted between the model and an external description.
No converse is claimed that every vacuum solution of the field law is isometric to this datum.

citations.quote:
Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Define the
smooth vector field

$$n:=f^{-1/2}\,\partial_0=\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1/2}\partial_0$$

on $M$. Then:

**(a) Observer congruence.** $n$ is a smooth observer congruence on $M$ in the
sense of [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]: $g(n,n)=-1$ and
$g(n,N)<0$ at every point, so $n$ is a future-directed unit timelike field.

**(b) Integral curves.** For any $p=(c_0,r_0,\omega_0)\in M$, including sphere poles, the maximal integral curve of $n$ through $p$, with length-valued flow parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, is
$$\lambda\mapsto\bigl(c_0+f(r_0)^{-1/2}\lambda,\ r_0,\ \omega_0\bigr).$$
It is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and is the **static observer worldline** at radius $r_0$. In a spherical-polar chart it has constant angular coordinates $(\vartheta_0,\varphi_0)$; in any angular chart the sphere point is constant, and the global coordinate $x^0$ increases monotonically.

**(c) Proper time and clock rate.** Along each static observer worldline the
proper time $\tau$ is an affine function of the flow parameter $\lambda$, with
$\frac{d\tau}{d\lambda}=\frac1c$, and

$$\Delta\tau=\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{c}\,\Delta x^0=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t,$$

where $\Delta x^0$ is the coordinate difference in metres between two events
of the worldline and $\Delta t=\Delta x^0/c$ is the same difference in
seconds. In particular the proper-time increment is strictly positive for
$\Delta x^0>0$, and it is smaller than $\Delta t$ at every finite radius
because $0<f(r_0)<1$.

**(d) Clock-rate ratio.** For two static observers at radii
$r_1,r_2\in(s,\infty)$ compared over the same coordinate interval
$\Delta x^0$, the proper-time increments satisfy

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_1}{\Delta\tau_2}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_1)}{f(r_2)}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-s/r_1}{1-s/r_2}} .$$

**(e) Acceleration.** The acceleration field of the congruence is
$a:=\nabla_nn=\frac{f'(r)}{2}\,\partial_1=\frac{s}{2r^2}\,\partial_r$; it is
spatial, nowhere zero, and points in the direction of increasing $r$, so the
static observers are not geodesics.

**(f) Scope.** These are identities of the geometric datum. The reading of
$\tau$ as the time measured by an ideal clock and of the congruence as a
family of static observers belongs to the framework's postulates and is not
asserted here; no measurement and no comparison with any observed rate is
made.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a **future
timelike geodesic**, parametrized by proper time $\tau$, with tangent
$U=\gamma'$, so that $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future-directed
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] clause 3,
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Fix a spherical-polar product chart
$(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ containing the image of $\gamma$ and write a dot
for $\frac{d}{d\tau}$. Define

$$e:=-g(U,\partial_0)=f\dot x^0,\qquad \ell:=g(U,\partial_\varphi)=r^2\sin^2\vartheta\,\dot\varphi .$$

Then:

**(a) Conserved quantities.** $\partial_0$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are Killing
fields of $g$, and $e$ and $\ell$ are constant along $\gamma$; moreover
$e>0$.

**(b) Equatorial reduction.** Suppose $\vartheta(\tau_0)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and
$\dot\vartheta(\tau_0)=0$ at some $\tau_0\in I$. Then
$\vartheta(\tau)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ for all $\tau\in I$; the geodesic is
**equatorial**.

**(c) Radial reduction.** If $\gamma$ is equatorial, define the **effective
potential**

$$W_\ell(r):=f(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr).$$

Then the normalization identity

$$\dot r^2=e^2-W_\ell(r)$$

holds at every $\tau\in I$, and, given this identity, the $r$-component of the
geodesic equation is equivalent to the one-dimensional equation

$$\ddot r=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),\qquad W_\ell'(r)=f'(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr)-2f(r)\frac{\ell^2}{r^3}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The reduction is local: it is stated on the interval $I$ on
which the geodesic stays in one product chart with $r>s$ and
$0<\vartheta<\pi$; no completeness, no extension of $\gamma$ beyond $I$, and
no statement about null geodesics is made. The quantities $e$ and $\ell$ are
constants of the given geodesic, not functions of the model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]), and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector
field with compact support whose flow $\Phi_v$ is a global flow
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose:

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(u,v)=S(g,\varphi)$ for all $(u,v)$ in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, let $n$ be an observer at $p$, and let $c>0$ be a real parameter
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observer energy and spatial momentum.** For every $P\in T_pM$ define the
**observer energy** and the **spatial momentum** of $P$ relative to $n$ by

$$E_n(P):=-c\,g_p(P,n),\qquad q_n(P):=h_n(P),$$

where $h_n$ is the spatial projection of the observer $n$. Both maps are
$\mathbb R$-linear in $P$: the first because $g_p$ is bilinear, the second by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The second takes values in the
rest space $n^{\perp}$, and by the rest-space decomposition of that lemma every
$P$ has the unique decomposition

$$P=\frac{E_n(P)}{c}\,n+q_n(P),\qquad \frac{E_n(P)}{c}\in\mathbb R,\quad q_n(P)\in n^{\perp}.$$

Equivalently $E_n(P)=c\,\lambda$ and $q_n(P)=w$ for the unique pair
$(\lambda,w)$ with $P=\lambda n+w$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $w\in n^{\perp}$.

**(b) Rest mass and four-velocity normalization.** For $P\in T_pM$ with
$g_p(P,P)\le0$ define the **rest mass**

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-g_p(P,P)}}{c}\ge0,$$

where the square root is the nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]. By
strict positivity of the square root of a positive number, $m(P)=0$ exactly
when $P=0$ or $P$ is null, and $m(P)>0$ exactly when $P$ is timelike
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). When $m(P)>0$, define the
**normalized four-velocity direction**

$$U(P):=\frac{P}{m(P)},$$

so that $g_p(U(P),U(P))=g_p(P,P)/m(P)^2=-c^2$. Conversely, if $m>0$ and
$U\in T_pM$ satisfy $g_p(U,U)=-c^2$, then $P:=mU$ has $g_p(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ and
$m(P)=m$, $U(P)=U$; the pair $(m,U)$ with $U$ future-directed determines and
is determined by its future timelike $P=mU$.

**(c) Scope and reading.** $E_n$ and $q_n$ depend on the observer $n$: for the
same nonzero $P$, different observers $n,n'$ generally give different values,
and no observer-independent splitting of $P$ into "energy" and "momentum" is
defined by this item. The identities above are algebraic; this definition
asserts no positivity of $E_n$ (that is proved separately), no conservation,
no dynamics and no measurement. The names observer energy, spatial momentum
and rest mass, and their physical units and interpretation, belong to the
physical reading of the framework's unit conventions and postulates and are
not asserted here; this item fixes only the mathematical dependence on the
objects $P$, $n$, $g_p$ and the parameter $c$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
